and Public Policy to Develop Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Systems DETAILED RESEARCH DESCRIPTION Overview The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), has fundamentally transformed the way humans acquire knowledge, communicate, learn, conduct research, solve problems, and make decisions. AI-powered systems such as ChatGPT and other advanced language models have become integral tools across education, healthcare, engineering, scientific research, finance, governance, software development, and creative industries. Their ability to generate human-like text, analyze complex information, write computer programs, summarize research, translate languages, and assist in decision-making has significantly enhanced productivity and accessibility to knowledge. Despite these remarkable advantages, increasing dependence on AI has raised important questions regarding the future of human intelligence and cognitive development. As individuals increasingly rely on AI to perform tasks that traditionally required reasoning, memory, creativity, and analytical thinking, concerns have emerged regarding cognitive offloading, reduced independent problem-solving, declining critical thinking, diminished originality, and excessive reliance on algorithmic decision-making. These concerns have stimulated interdisciplinary research across cognitive psychology, neuroscience, education, human–computer interaction, ethics, and public policy. This research presents a comprehensive multidisciplinary review of AI dependency and its influence on human cognitive development. It synthesizes contemporary literature to examine the opportunities and challenges associated with widespread AI adoption while emphasizing that AI should function as an augmentative technology that strengthens rather than replaces human intelligence. The study critically evaluates cognitive offloading mechanisms, human memory processes, creativity, metacognition, educational transformation, digital literacy, and ethical decision-making in AI-assisted environments. A central contribution of this research is the development of a Human–AI Collaboration Framework, which integrates human cognitive strengths—including creativity, ethical reasoning, contextual understanding, emotional intelligence, and critical thinking—with AI capabilities such as large-scale data processing, knowledge retrieval, automation, predictive analytics, and intelligent decision support. The framework demonstrates that sustainable technological progress depends on complementary collaboration between humans and AI rather than technological substitution. The paper also explores the implications of AI dependency for education and workforce development. It discusses how universities, schools, research institutions, industries, and governments can integrate AI responsibly by redesigning curricula, promoting AI literacy, strengthening critical thinking, encouraging experiential learning, and fostering ethical awareness. Special attention is given to preserving originality, scientific integrity, and lifelong learning while leveraging AI to enhance educational outcomes. Furthermore, the study investigates broader societal issues including algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, privacy, explainability, digital governance, intellectual property, and responsible innovation. It examines international AI governance initiatives and proposes policy recommendations for ensuring that AI remains transparent, trustworthy, inclusive, and aligned with human values. By integrating insights from multiple disciplines, the paper contributes to ongoing discussions surrounding Responsible Artificial Intelligence, Explainable AI (XAI), and Human-Centered AI. The proposed framework introduces a conceptual AI Dependency Model that categorizes different levels of AI reliance, ranging from minimal assistance to excessive dependency. The model highlights the importance of maintaining an optimal balance where AI enhances productivity and decision-making while preserving independent reasoning, creativity, and cognitive resilience. This balanced approach supports sustainable innovation and reduces the risks associated with overdependence on intelligent technologies. The findings emphasize that future AI systems should be designed to complement human intelligence by encouraging critical evaluation, reflective thinking, ethical judgment, and collaborative problem-solving. Educational institutions should integrate AI as a learning partner rather than a replacement for intellectual effort, while policymakers should establish governance mechanisms that ensure fairness, transparency, accountability, and responsible deployment across sectors. Ultimately, this research argues that the future of Artificial Intelligence should not be measured solely by computational performance or automation capabilities, but by its ability to enhance human potential, strengthen cognitive development, promote ethical decision-making, and contribute to sustainable societal progress. Human-centered AI offers a pathway toward technological innovation that preserves the uniquely human qualities of creativity, empathy, wisdom, and moral responsibility while harnessing the transformative power of intelligent machines. title: From Navigation Tool to Persistent Memory: Graphical Memory Systems for Long-Term LLM Recall
authors: H W Yang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Our prior work demonstrated that dependency graphs improve cross-module bug fixing (Phase 1 [1]) and that topic-relationship graphs enable efficient long-conversation navigation (Phase 2 [2]). However, in both phases, the graph served as an external tool—a map the model consulted before returning to the “primary storage” of raw text. This paper introduces Graphical Memory Systems: a paradigm where the graph is the memory. Instead of generating disposable navigation aids, the model maintains a persistent, incrementally-updated “memory canvas” where each conversation session adds nodes, edges, annotations, and comments that survive across time. We structure the investigation into two layers: Layer 1—Feasibility (Phase 3a): four zero-training concept-validation experiments testing whether a multi-modal model can read memory graphs as a primary information source, measuring recall accuracy, token efficiency, and annotation utility against full-text retrieval. Layer 2—Agency (Phase 3b): split into tool-calling (3b-1)—can models be trained to actively invoke memory-graph tools during conversation?—and internalization (3b-2)—does the graphical-memory habit persist when tools are removed? We release memory graph, an open-source toolchain extending Phase 2’s cognitivesketch with persistent incremental memory graphs.

title: Lost in the PDFs: Context Degradation and Parametric Hallucinations in LLM UIs
authors: Gabriele
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This record contains the preprint paper "LOST IN THE PDFS: CONTEXT DEGRADATION AND PARAMETRIC HALLUCINATIONS IN LLM UIS", authored by Gabriele D’Iorio (University of Naples Parthenope). The study investigates the structural limitations and operational vulnerabilities of commercial web-based Large Language Model (LLM) interfaces when handling long, multi-document sequential workflows in educational contexts. Abstract:The growing use of LLMs for educational purposes, especially by inexperienced users, inevitably leads to LLMs hallucinating and making mistakes. This study presents an experiment using the web version of Gemini (Pro Standard and Flash Standard modes) to simulate a numerical analysis class covering three topics (interpolation, piecewise interpolation, and approximation), each in a separate PDF. This study is subdivided into two scenarios created to evaluate how the LLM responded and, above all, to see how long it took to hallucinate or suffer from context degradation. The results demonstrate the failure of both scenarios due to context degradation. Despite large theoretical context windows, sudden attachment truncation in the web UI forces the model to rely on its parametric memory, leading to severe hallucinations and sycophantic behavior. Key Topics Covered:- Context Degradation & "Lost in the Middle" Phenomenon: Analysis of how LLMs lose retrieval accuracy in prolonged sessions.- Parametric Hallucinations: How models compensate for context loss by fabricating details from pre-training data.- Document Parsing Challenges: Visual layout issues in standard Web UIs.- Experimental Evaluation: A comparative analysis of a single-chat setup (Scenario A) versus a dual-agent/tutor setup (Scenario B). Data Availability:The comprehensive dataset, interaction logs, prompt configurations, and Python scripts used for token counting are openly accessible in the project’s GitHub repository at: https://github.com/g-projectech/lost_in_the_pdfs/

title: The Capacity Knee: Pricing the Working State of a Language Model — A Two-Part Law, and the Break that Measures the Reader
authors: Nathan Ryan Young
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: How many things can a language model hold in mind at once? Treating the readout-invisible component of pythia-410m's residual stream as a storage channel and superposing n independent operand cargoes in its functional subspace, this paper measures a two-part law. Content is CONSERVED: the summed content-differential survives to n=64 — amplitude superposition without collapse. Delivery is SLOT-BOUNDED: the fraction of cargoes individually recoverable above a null-calibrated threshold breaks at a knee (n*=4 and 6 on two seed lineages), giving a reliable working-state capacity of about TWO items. A derivation committed to the repository BEFORE the experiment predicts the mechanism — signal-to-interference SIR^2(n) = D_eff/(n-1) — and the knee inverts into an instrument: D_eff = 11.1 and 14.3, a dozen effective coordinates, matching the independently measured width of the operand code. A full-amplitude control confirms the break is genuine cross-talk, not amplitude starvation. The scale ladder (pythia 1b to 2.8b) refused its gates honestly and is shipped as the void it is, with two textures at full weight: no ladder capacity bound exceeds ~2 slots, and the read SUPERLINEARIZES with scale. A gentle-injection retry maps the cross-family dose-response and closes that sub-line as instrument-bounded (gentle windows exist at single-cargo level; no dose survives the full ladder). A reader-versus-medium experiment sharpens the attribution: an optimal codebook-equipped external reader breaks at the same knee — the limit lives in the carried code, not the readout — and the READABLE channel externally carries as much working state as the dark one, making wider auditable working memory a write-side engineering target. Sealed branch predictions with gates git-committed before build; misses banked at full weight. Companion verification deposit (including the pre-run derivation document, verbatim): deposit 0l. Methods and drafting in close collaboration with Claude (Anthropic), disclosed throughout; every number traces to a sealed, pre-registered run.

title: Engagement in Code Review: Emotional, Behavioral, and Cognitive Dimensions in Peer vs. LLM Interactions
authors: Adam Alami; Nathan Cassee; Thiago Rocha Silva; Elda Paja; Neil Ernst
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: Code review is a socio-technical practice, yet how software engineers engage in Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted code reviews compared to human peer-led reviews is less understood, especially as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. We report a two-phase qualitative study with 20 software engineers to understand such dynamics. In Phase I, participants exchanged peer reviews and were interviewed about their affective responses and engagement decisions. We also prompted them to discuss their submitted code review generated by ChatGPT 4o. In Phase II, we investigated and introduced a new prompt to match engineers’ stated preferences for the review and probed how content characteristics shaped their reactions. We develop an integrative account linking emotional self-regulation to behavioral engagement and likelihood of a resolution. We identify a repertoire of participant-reported self-regulation strategies that engineers use to regulate their emotions in response to negative feedback: reframing, dialogic regulation, avoidance, and defensiveness. These strategies are inspired by the engineers’ commitment to code quality and values: accountability and growth mindset. Engagement proceeds through social calibration; engineers seem to align their responses and behaviors to the relational climate and team norms. Trajectories to likelihood of a resolution, in the case of peer-led review, vary by locus (solo/dyad/team) and an internal sense-making process. With the LLM-assisted review, emotional costs and the need for self-regulation seem lower, as reported by participants in our sample. When LLM feedback appear to better align with engineers’ cognitive expectations (e.g., clear structure, concise scope, neutral tone, actionable), participants reported reduced processing effort and a potentially higher tendency to adopt. As reported by our participants, our findings demonstrate that LLM-assisted review redirects engagement from managing emotions and social affect to managing cognitive load. We contribute with an integrative model of engagement, linking emotional self-regulation \(\leftrightarrow\) behavioral engagement \(\rightarrow\) likelihood to a resolution, showing how affective and cognitive processes may influence feedback adoption in peer-led and LLM-assisted code reviews. We conclude that AI is best positioned as a supportive partner to potentially reduce cognitive and emotional load while preserving human accountability and the social meaning of peer review and similar socio-technical activities.

title: TOPO-2026: A Universal Framework for Continual Learning, Bias Elimination, and World Model Certification in Large Language Models and Vision Systems
authors: FRANK MORALES
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: TOPO-2026 is a universal certification framework designed to address three persistent barriers in AI: catastrophic forgetting, AI bias, and world model instability. It utilizes prime-anchored embedding invariants—derived from Arithmetic Spectral Theory (AST)—to provide mathematical guarantees for memory preservation, bias elimination, and world model certification. Core Mechanisms The framework operates by fixing a sparse set of reference embedding rows at prime indices {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13}. This ensures $O(1)$ memory overhead, requiring only 451.5 KB to protect 124 billion parameters—an overhead of just 0.00000036%. Key functional components include: TOPO: Solves catastrophic forgetting through prime-anchored invariants, providing a mathematical guarantee of memory preservation. TOPO-BIAS: Eliminates AI bias via a four-tier spectral annihilation framework, making biased associations geometrically unconstructable. TOPO-JEPA: Integrates the TOPO framework with JEPA’s predictive world models, resulting in zero-forgetting, stable, and equitable world models. Performance and Stability The framework has been validated across six distinct production architectures, ranging from dense transformers and sparse Mixture-of-Experts to vision transformers. Memory Preservation: Demonstrated 100% Task C accuracy with 0.0% forgetting on Gemma-4-E4B-Vision and consistent results across other models like DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Sarvam-30B. Bias Elimination: Achieved a 100% bias rejection rate. Numerical Stability: Recorded zero NaN/Inf events across 1.99 billion embedding elements. World Model Efficiency: TOPO-JEPA achieved negative forgetting (-0.75%) with 89.0% accuracy, using 34,000 times less memory than the HOPE architecture. Auditability and Availability To ensure deterministic, verifiable performance, the framework uses a seed of 123 and provides cryptographic auditability via SHA-256 hashes. The complete, open-source framework is accessible through the Sovereign Machine Laboratory (SOMALA) archives, including the code repository and documentation.

title: Mixture-of-Experts in Large Language Models: A Survey of Architecture, Training, and Efficient Inference
authors: Abeda Elhenawy
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AbstractThe scaling of large language models (LLMs) along the parameter-count axis has produced remarkable capability gains, but ithas also produced a proportional increase in inference compute—a constraint that limits deployment to organisations with sub-stantial GPU resources. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer a way out of this impasse by activating only a subset of modelparameters per token, thereby decoupling total parameter count from per-token compute. This survey presents a comprehensivesynthesis of MoE techniques in LLMs organised along four pillars: (i) architectural approaches, covering routing mechanisms(top-𝑘, expert-choice, soft merging), expert designs (homogeneous, fine-grained, shared, hierarchical), and the placement ofMoE within attention versus feed-forward layers; (ii) training methodologies, covering load-balancing auxiliary losses, expertcollapse mitigation, data routing, and fine-tuning strategies (MoE-LoRA, expert freezing, mixture-of-LoRA); (iii) inference op-timization, covering the memory wall, expert offloading and quantization (QMoE), dynamic routing speedup, expert-parallelbatching, and multi-GPU tensor-parallel inference; and (iv) evaluation and applications, spanning Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE,Qwen-MoE, Kimi-MoE, multimodal MoE (MoE-LLaVA), and edge MoE. We propose a four-axis taxonomy that subsumes ex-isting framings and synthesise the rapidly growing literature from the original sparsely-gated MoE [34] through the open-weightMoE revolution of 2024–2026. We further analyse the principal open problems—routing instability, the memory–computetrade-off, expert interpretability, fine-tuning instability, distributed training cost, and multimodal fusion—and outline futuredirections centred on native 1-bit MoE, expert merging, reasoning-oriented MoE, hardware co-design, and theoretical under-standing. The survey covers literature from January 2017 through July 2026.Keywords: Mixture-of-Experts; Sparse Expert Models; Conditional Computation; Mixtral; DeepSeek-MoE; Large LanguageModels; Efficient Inference; Survey Introduction The rapid maturation of large language models (LLMs) following the introduction of the transformer architecture and the demonstration of emergent in-context capabilities at scale has prompted a fundamental rethinking of what artificial intelligence systems can do. Whereas the previous decade of deep learning was dominated by discriminative models trained for narrow tasks—image classification, speech recognition, sentiment analysis—the current decade is increasingly defined by generative models that produce fluent text, code, and structured reasoning across domains they were never explicitly trained on. Yet fluency alone does not amount to intelligence in any practically useful sense. A model that merely predicts the next token, however skilfully, remains a passive instrument: it generates, but it does not act. The shift from passive generation to active intervention is the defining move of agentic AI. An AI agent, in the sense now crystallising across the research literature, is a system that perceives its environment, reasons about what it has perceived, and takes actions that reshape that environment in pursuit of a goal. The distinction between an LLM and an LLM-based agent is not merely terminological. A bare language model produces a single output and stops; an agent produces a trajectory—a sequence of decisions unfolding across time, responsive to a world that pushes back, capable of failure, retry, and adaptation. This trajectory is what closes the gap between text generation and genuine autonomy. The agent paradigm crystallised with remarkable speed. The release of AutoGPT in March 2023—an experimental system that chained GPT-4 prompts to pursue long-horizon goals with minimal human intervention—became the fastest-growing repository in GitHub's history and signalled that the broader research community and the public were ready to take the agentic idea seriously. Within months, frameworks such as BabyAGI, LangChain, AutoGen, and CrewAI had proliferated, each offering scaffolding for multi-step agent workflows. By 2024, autonomous software engineers such as Devin demonstrated end-to-end completion of real Upwork jobs, and by 2025–2026 general-purpose agents such as Manus and the broader ecosystem of OS-level assistants had entered mainstream use. The term "agentic AI" is now widely used to denote the defining frontier of the field. Despite this rapid progress, the field suffers from conceptual fragmentation. Surveys published as recently as 2023 predate the explosion of multi-agent frameworks and the standardisation of tool-calling APIs. More recent surveys have begun to systematise the territory, but no single work simultaneously covers architectural components, benchmarks, deployments, and open problems at the depth required by both researchers and practitioners. This survey addresses that gap Contributions of this Work This paper makes four principal contributions to the conditional computation and sparse architecture literature: A Four-Axis Strategic Taxonomy: We propose a comprehensive structural taxonomy that categorizes modern sparse language models along orthogonal axes: Routing Granularity, Expert Specialization, Load Balancing Strategy, and Deployment Target. Deep Breakdown of Routing & Expert Engineering: We provide a rigorous comparative dissection of contemporary gating mechanisms (top-$k$, expert-choice, soft merging) and advanced expert layout configurations (fine-grained, shared, and hierarchical models) (Section 5). Synthesis of Inference Acceleration & Hardware Optimization: We systematically analyze the mitigation strategies designed to address the unique memory bottlenecks of sparse execution, covering predictive expert offloading, sub-byte quantization ($\text{QMoE}$), and expert-parallel batching runtimes (Section 7). Open Challenges and Research Frontiers: We isolate the structural constraints currently limiting production $\text{MoE}$ deployment—including routing instabilities, the memory wall, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and distributed training constraints—and outline a cross-pollinated roadmap toward native $1\text{-bit}$ sparse architectures (Sections 9–10)

title: ProjectMind: An Evidence-Frontier and Authority-Governed Project Continuity Architecture for AI Coding Agents
authors: Agim Haxhijaha
abstract: ProjectMind is a proposed local-first project-continuity and evidence-governance architecture for AI-assisted software development. For a target Git commit it computes a canonical Evidence Frontier, maintains claims with separate authenticity, confidence, authority, freshness, and completeness dimensions, records authority changes in an append-only ledger, and compiles task-specific knowledge into an immutable Change Consequence Contract. After a candidate is frozen, it independently reconstructs and reconciles the observed project-state and test delta and emits a Continuity Receipt. The proposal builds on established code graphs, temporal agent memory, impact analysis, MCP, provenance, policy, and attestation systems. Its contribution is the linked commit-DAG continuity-control chain, not the novelty of those components individually. This publication does not claim implementation, validation, patentability, legal compliance, peer review, certification, or production readiness.

title: ficient Large Language Models: A Survey of Quantization, Pruning, Distillation, and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
authors: Abeda Elhenawy
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AbstractThe emergence of large language models (LLMs) with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters has produced remarkablecapabilities in reasoning, code generation, and multi-step problem solving, but has simultaneously created a severe deploymentbottleneck: the compute, memory, and energy requirements of these models place them beyond the reach of most academic,small-firm, and edge-deployment scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of efficient LLM techniques organised along four pillars: (i) quantization, which reduces the numerical precision of weights, activations, and the KV cache; (ii)pruning and sparsity, which removes redundant parameters or structures; (iii) knowledge distillation, which transfers competence from large teacher models to smaller students; and (iv) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), which adapts pretrainedmodels to downstream tasks by training only a small fraction of their parameters. We propose a taxonomy that organises thesetechniques along four orthogonal axes—compression stage, granularity, parameter footprint, and deployment target—and synthesise the rapidly growing literature on methods including GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, SparseGPT, Wanda, Sheared LLaMA,DistilBERT lineage, Phi-3, LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, and prefix tuning. We further survey the deployment infrastructure (vLLM,TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, MLC-LLM) that translates algorithmic efficiency into measurable production gains, and analyse theprincipal open problems: accuracy degradation under aggressive compression, calibration data sensitivity, hardware co-design,and standardised evaluation. The survey covers literature from January 2020 through July 2026 and is structured to serve as areference for researchers, practitioners, and hardware architects engaging with the efficient-LLM frontier.Keywords: Large Language Models; Model Compression; Quantization; Pruning; Knowledge Distillation; Parameter-EfficientFine-Tuning; LoRA; Efficient Inference; Survey Here is the fully completed, publication-ready Introduction for your second survey paper, "Efficient Large Language Models: A Survey of Quantization, Pruning, Distillation, and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques". This version resolves the missing citation placeholder [?] by integrating the seminal models of that scale (GPT-3, PaLM, LLaMA) and standardizes all technical units using precise LaTeX formatting. 1. Introduction The last five years of natural language processing have been defined by a single trajectory: larger models, trained on larger datasets, with larger compute budgets, yield qualitatively better capabilities. The scaling laws established by Kaplan et al. [30] and refined by Hoffmann et al. [24] demonstrated that model loss decreases as a predictable power law in parameters and data, a finding that motivated the construction of dense models with hundreds of billions of parameters—such as GPT-3 ($175\text{B}$), PaLM ($540\text{B}$), and LLaMA ($70\text{B}$)—and eventually trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts architectures [1, 14, 24, 30, 59]. The downstream effects of this massive scaling—including emergent in-context learning, multi-turn chain-of-thought reasoning, autonomous code generation, and complex multi-step tool use—have fundamentally reshaped the entire landscape of artificial intelligence. Yet, this trajectory has simultaneously produced a deployment bottleneck of considerable severity. A $70\text{-billion}$-parameter model running in standard half-precision ($\text{FP16}$) requires approximately $140\text{ GB}$ of graphics processing unit ($\text{GPU}$) memory just to load its underlying weights, and substantially more once active inference activations, the key-value ($\text{KV}$) cache, and operational state parameters are accounted for [2, 9]. Scaling up further, the $175\text{-billion}$-parameter GPT-3 requires approximately $350\text{ GB}$, while the dense $540\text{-billion}$-parameter PaLM demands more than a terabyte of high-bandwidth memory. These massive resource footprints effectively place state-of-the-art models entirely beyond the reach of most academic laboratories, small-and-medium enterprises ($\text{SMEs}$), and consumer edge-deployment scenarios characterized by strict latency, energy, or operational cost constraints [50, 55]. The centralized, cloud-based $\text{API}$ business model that has emerged around contemporary frontier models—wherein users pay a recurring cost per token to query a black-box model—is, in part, a market response to the sheer economic and hardware impossibility of local, decentralized deployment at this scale. The global research community has responded to this challenge with a rapidly accelerating body of work dedicated to efficient LLM techniques. These methodologies aim to dramatically reduce the compute, memory, and energy footprint of large models without proportionally degrading their core cognitive and linguistic capabilities. As illustrated in modern literature, these engineering techniques primarily fall into four foundational technical pillars: Quantization: Reduces the numerical precision of model weights, activations, or the $\text{KV}$ cache from standard $16\text{-bit}$ floating point to $8\text{-bit}$, $4\text{-bit}$, $3\text{-bit}$, or even sub-byte ($1\text{-bit}$ or $1.58\text{-bit}$) architectures, yielding memory reductions roughly proportional to bit-width compression [9, 14, 39, 45]. Pruning and Sparsity: Identifies and systematically removes structurally redundant parameters, attention heads, layers, or sub-networks while preserving the model's essential functional behavior [15, 57, 58]. Knowledge Distillation: Replicates and transfers compressed cognitive competence from a massive "teacher" model to a highly compact, structurally optimized "student" architecture designed specifically for local runtime environments [23, 36, 54]. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT): Freezes the multi-billion parameter base model and restricts downstream task adaptation to a tiny fraction of auxiliary trainable weights (typically $<1\%$), drastically dropping fine-tuning memory thresholds [10, 28, 40]. Despite this rapid surge in algorithmic progress, the field continues to suffer from severe conceptual fragmentation. Comprehensive efficiency surveys published as recently as 2023 [71] predate the structural maturity of stable $4\text{-bit}$ post-training quantization methods and the widespread standardization of optimization ecosystems in mainstream open-source libraries. While more recent specialized surveys have begun to systematize distinct domains [62, 65], no single comprehensive work simultaneously synthesizes all four core technical pillars alongside practical deployment runtime infrastructure ($\text{vLLM}$, $\text{TensorRT-LLM}$, $\text{llama.cpp}$, $\text{MLC-LLM}$) and empirical hardware trade-offs at the granular depth required by both academic researchers and systems architects. This survey explicitly addresses that gap. Contributions of this Work This paper makes four principal contributions to the model compression and acceleration literature: A Unified Technical Taxonomy: We propose a comprehensive, four-axis taxonomy that organizes LLM efficiency techniques along orthogonal operational dimensions: Compression Stage, Granularity, Parameter Footprint, and Deployment Target. Architectural Dissection of the Four Pillars: We provide a rigorous comparative breakdown of modern quantization, pruning, distillation, and $\text{PEFT}$ frameworks, establishing direct cross-method analytical frameworks (Sections 5–8). Synthesis of Deployment Runtime Infrastructure: We evaluate the state-of-the-art inference engines that translate theoretical algorithmic compression into measurable hardware throughput and token latency gains across heterogeneous platforms (Section 10). Open Challenges and Research Roadmap: We map out the binding constraints of current compression paradigms—such as reasoning degradation under sub-byte quantizations, calibration data dependencies, and the evaluation crisis—and project a structural roadmap for future hardware-software co-design (Sections 11–12).

title: Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey of Vision-Language Integration, Architectures, and Applications
authors: Abeda Elhenawy
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AbstractThe extension of large language models (LLMs) from purely textual inputs to multimodal inputs—images, video, audio, andstructured data—represents one of the most consequential transitions in contemporary artificial intelligence. Multimodal largelanguage models (MLLMs) such as GPT-4V, Gemini, Claude 3 Vision, and the open-weight LLaVA family have demon-strated that a single pretrained model can perform visual question answering, document understanding, chart interpretation,and grounded reasoning at levels approaching human competence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of MLLMsorganised along four pillars: (i) architectural approaches, contrasting contrastive alignment (CLIP, ALIGN), generative vision-language models (Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA), and native multimodal pretraining (GPT-4V, Gemini); (ii) training methodolo-gies, covering multimodal pretraining data (LAION-5B, DataComp), visual instruction tuning (LLaVA-Instruct, ShareGPT4V),and multimodal RLHF (RLAIF-V, RLHF-V); (iii) evaluation benchmarks, including general VQA, knowledge-intensive VQA,chart/document understanding, multimodal reasoning (MMMU, MathVista), and hallucination metrics (POPE, Hallusion-Bench); and (iv) applications, spanning document intelligence, medical imaging, autonomous driving, robotics, and GUI agents.We propose a four-axis taxonomy of MLLM architectures and synthesise the rapidly growing literature on connector designs(Q-Former, MLP projector, cross-attention), modality fusion strategies, and LLM freezing regimes. We further analyse the prin-cipal open problems—object hallucination, modality gap, reasoning-versus-recognition gap, data quality and licensing, safetyconcerns, and computational cost—and outline future directions centred on native multimodal pretraining, video understanding,embodied reasoning, and standardised evaluation. The survey covers literature from January 2021 through July 2026.Keywords: Multimodal Large Language Models; Vision-Language Models; Visual Instruction Tuning; Multimodal Reasoning;Object Hallucination; CLIP; LLaVA; Survey 1 Introduction The rapid maturation of large language models (LLMs) following the introduction of the transformer architecture and the demonstration of emergent in-context capabilities at scale has prompted a fundamental rethinking of what artificial intelligence systems can do. Whereas the previous decade of deep learning was dominated by discriminative models trained for narrow tasks—image classification, speech recognition, sentiment analysis—the current decade is increasingly defined by generative models that produce fluent text, code, and structured reasoning across domains they were never explicitly trained on. Yet fluency alone does not amount to intelligence in any practically useful sense. A model that merely predicts the next token, however skilfully, remains a passive instrument: it generates, but it does not act. The shift from passive generation to active intervention is the defining move of agentic AI. An AI agent, in the sense now crystallising across the research literature, is a system that perceives its environment, reasons about what it has perceived, and takes actions that reshape that environment in pursuit of a goal. The distinction between an LLM and an LLM-based agent is not merely terminological. A bare language model produces a single output and stops; an agent produces a trajectory—a sequence of decisions unfolding across time, responsive to a world that pushes back, capable of failure, retry, and adaptation. This trajectory is what closes the gap between text generation and genuine autonomy. The agent paradigm crystallised with remarkable speed. The release of AutoGPT in March 2023—an experimental system that chained GPT-4 prompts to pursue long-horizon goals with minimal human intervention—became the fastest-growing repository in GitHub's history and signalled that the broader research community and the public were ready to take the agentic idea seriously. Within months, frameworks such as BabyAGI, LangChain, AutoGen, and CrewAI had proliferated, each offering scaffolding for multi-step agent workflows. By 2024, autonomous software engineers such as Devin demonstrated end-to-end completion of real Upwork jobs, and by 2025–2026 general-purpose agents such as Manus and the broader ecosystem of OS-level assistants had entered mainstream use. The term "agentic AI" is now widely used to denote the defining frontier of the field. Despite this rapid progress, the field suffers from conceptual fragmentation. Surveys published as recently as 2023 predate the explosion of multi-agent frameworks and the standardisation of tool-calling APIs. More recent surveys have begun to systematise the territory, but no single work simultaneously covers architectural components, benchmarks, deployments, and open problems at the depth required by both researchers and practitioners. This survey addresses that gap. Contributions This paper makes four contributions: Taxonomy: We propose a four-axis taxonomy of agentic AI systems that subsumes existing framings and accommodates emerging architectures (Section 4). Synthesis: We disassemble and synthesize the core architectural components—perception, memory, planning, tool use, and multi-agent coordination—into a unified reference framework (Section 5). Evaluation Benchmarks: We provide a comparative analysis of the major agentic benchmarks and identify their structural limitations (Section 6). Challenges & Roadmap: We map the principal open problems and outline a research roadmap spanning world models, continual learning, evaluation, and governance (Sections 8–9). Organisation The remainder of this survey is structured to facilitate systematically navigating the agentic landscape. Section 2 traces the genealogy from symbolic AI to modern LLM agents. Section 3 describes our survey methodology. Sections 4–7 present the taxonomy, architecture, benchmarks, and real-world applications. Sections 8–9 analyze open problems and future directions. Section 11 concludes the paper

title: The Scaffold Continuity Trap: A Blinded Scaffold-Lesion Test in Persistent Coding Agents
authors: Thomas Ryan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Persistent AI agents can appear to continue projects, commitments, and working identity across sessions. This preprint tests whether continuity-like behavior in a coding-agent continuation task is carried by external scaffolds such as project files, tests, handoff notes, summaries, tool traces, and control state. The study uses a blinded scaffold-lesion protocol with four separate blinded runner threads assigned to primary straight-condition packets: full scaffold, summary-only, no-memory, and sham lesion. All four achieved 12/12 on the core continuation score. The preregistered full-versus-no-memory gate therefore failed: the observed core-score delta was 0.0 against a required 3/12-point threshold. The full-versus-summary comparison also failed, while sham stability passed. Hidden-probe recovery remained low across conditions. The result does not support the Scaffold Continuity Trap as originally stated for this fixture. The stronger bounded conclusion is narrower: in small coding-continuation tasks, ordinary visible repository state and tests can carry enough task-local causal structure for perfect action-level recovery even when richer continuity scaffolds are removed. Self-report continuity varied with scaffold richness, but task success did not. This work does not test or claim AI consciousness, personhood, moral status, survival, or subjective continuity. It is a scaffold-localization and methodology result about observable task continuation under controlled lesions.

title: Failure By Design - AI-Industry The Probabilistic Deficit: Empirical Measurement of Technical Debt, Economic Opacity, and Cognitive Atrophy in LLM-Driven Workflows
authors: Udo Granops
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into software engineering and critical infrastructure has been driven by vendor consensus and artificial benchmarks, masking a profound systemic failure. This meta-study synthesizes longitudinal raw telemetry, CI/CD artifacts, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and neuroimaging to bypass subjective sentiment surveys and expose the net-negative productivity loops of LLM-driven workflows. We identify a fundamental ontological mismatch: LLMs are probabilistic next-token predictors optimized for linguistic fluency, not semantic comprehension or logical correctness. Applying these statistical text-generators to zero-error engineering environments has triggered a triad of structural deficits. Economically, proprietary providers extract capital through opaque “idle meter” billing, background loops, and silent model downgrades, financially incentivizing failure-and-retry cycles over single-shot resolution. Technically, the illusion of rapid drafting is erased by a severe “review/rework tax.” Alarmingly, 24.2% of AI-introduced vulnerabilities survive into production due to automation bias and soft CI/CD gating. Cognitively, the outsourcing of productive cognitive friction to algorithmic generation measurably degrades human enactive neuroplasticity. EEG telemetry and longitudinal data reveal a widening skill gap between domain-master engineers and superficial “prompters,” accelerating a trajectory toward a macro-economic “knowledge-collapse steady state.” We conclude that the current Generative AI paradigm constitutes a compounding global infrastructure risk. To mitigate this, we propose immediate institutional directives: the mandatory unbundling of API billing, strict human-expert hard-gating for critical systems, a transition to deterministic fixed-cost computing, and a systemic reallocation of research funding toward verifiable, neuro-symbolic AI architectures.

title: Research on Early Stopping during Inference: Inference-Time Computing Flow Optimization via Reasoning Redundancy Elimination (RRE)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting techniques, the accuracy of models in handling complex logical reasoning, mathematical theorems, and code generation has been significantly improved. However, this "thinking" mechanism, which trades longer reasoning steps for higher performance, inevitably introduces immense computational resource consumption during autoregressive decoding. In practical scenarios, models frequently suffer from the "reasoning redundancy" phenomenon, falling into repetitive logical loops, divergent invalid arguments, or generating a plethora of superfluous tokens irrelevant to the final answer. This drastically inflates Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and generation costs per token, thereby hindering the feasibility of real-world deployment. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a non-intrusive early stopping framework named Reasoning Redundancy Elimination (RRE) for the inference phase. Without modifying the original parameters of the model, RRE introduces a lightweight dual-detection architecture during the decoding stage: the Semantic State Repetition Detector (SSRD) and the Dynamic Information Gain Evaluator (DIGE), which dynamically monitor the semantic trajectory and latent computational value of the generated reasoning steps. Once a reasoning segment is classified as low-value repetition, an invalid dead-end loop, or has reached a state of information convergence, RRE immediately sends an early stopping signal to the decoder, trims the redundant KV cache, and forces the model to jump directly to the final answer generation. Theoretical derivations and computational boundary analyses demonstrate that RRE substantially curtails invalid reasoning lengths and cuts down computational FLOPs exponentially while maintaining, or even improving, the final reasoning accuracy by eliminating error cascades in long-context generation. This framework offers a novel and promising paradigm for the highly efficient deployment of large language models.

title: SAGE: Solver-Aligned Guided Exploration
authors: Nikita Sorokin; Ivan Sedykh; Timur Ionov; Valentin Malykh
abstract: Modern code agents achieve strong results on challenging software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench, but solving each issue remains expensive: most inference cost is spent not on patch generation, but on repository exploration and search, accounting for up to 56% of tokens in our experiments. We propose SAGE, a modular approach that trains a small searcher model to handle codebase exploration as a tool for a frozen large solver model. We first distill the search trajectories from a strong agent to obtain a compact searcher with comparable retrieval quality. We then apply reinforcement learning to optimize the searcher for usefulness under the solver's fixed interface, using step-level feedback that directly evaluates whether retrieved context is actionable for downstream patching. On SWE-bench Verified, SAGE improves resolve rate while reducing search overhead by 67% and overall cost by 21%, demonstrating a practical path to cheaper, modular software engineering agents.

title: <p data-opencli-ref="202">DepthSketch-KV: Query-Conditioned Cross-Layer Residual Sketches for Long-Context KV Cache Compression
authors: Anna Córdoba; Adam Puente Tercero; Nerea Angulo Hijo; Mar Linares Tercero; Julia Barrientos
abstract: Long-context language model inference is increasingly limited by the memory footprint and bandwidth cost of KV caches, especially when retrieval-heavy prompts require preserving information across many layers. We introduce DepthSketch-KV, a cache compression method that exploits cross-layer redundancy by storing a shared low-rank residual sketch for adjacent transformer layers together with small per-layer key and value corrections. During decoding, query-conditioned depth gates estimate attention drift and choose whether each layer should access its local full-rank cache, the shared compressed cache, or a mixed reconstruction. A calibration-free error controller converts logit drift into per-sequence cache budgets, avoiding task-specific tuning while adapting to heterogeneous prompts. Across LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, NarrativeQA, Qasper, HotpotQA, GovReport, MultiNews, HumanEval, and MBPP, DepthSketch-KV consistently reduces KV cache memory at 32k and 64k contexts while preserving retrieval, QA, summarization, and code completion accuracy. Compared with MiniCache, H2O, StreamingLLM, SnapKV, PyramidKV, KIVI, and FlexGen, it improves the accuracy-memory tradeoff, increases decoding throughput, and reduces time to first token with only small changes in perplexity.

title: Amnesiac-Compatible Software Engineering: Failure-Class Lifecycle Governance for AI-Maintained Codebases
authors: Mayk Loide Baccaro
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This preprint introduces Amnesiac-Compatible Software Engineering (ACSE), a repository design pattern for AI-maintained codebases. ACSE treats future coding agents as competent but memory-volatile, and converts observed failures, stale claims, audit findings, and repeated review burdens into executable repository memory: failure classes, guard registries, deterministic controls, negative controls, claim-strength ledgers, bounded routing metadata, and companion artifacts. The upload includes the paper PDF.
