title: Enhancing Real-Time Drilling Decision Making Through a Customized LLM for Operational Reasoning and Knowledge Integration
authors: A. A. Kamal; M. F. Rahim; Hussen Mansur; W. Wan Aziz; B. Keong
abstract: Abstract Real-time drilling operations generate vast streams of data that must be interpreted and acted upon within seconds to ensure safe, efficient, and compliant well execution. Monitoring Specialists (MS) operating from Real-Time Centers (RTCs) face increasing operational complexity as modern wells incorporate deeper targets, narrower drilling margins, extended-reach trajectories, higher pressures and temperatures, and elevated operational risks. These conditions impose significant cognitive load on MS, particularly when rapid decisions require simultaneous consultation of multiple Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Standing Instructions for Drilling (SID), historical intervention records, and lessons learned stored across fragmented repositories. As operational expectations intensify, the ability of MS to rapidly retrieve, correlate, and contextualize technical knowledge has become a critical determinant of drilling effectiveness, Non-Productive Time (NPT) mitigation, and operational safety. However, existing digital oilfield tools, while effective in anomaly detection or trend monitoring, typically operate in isolation and depend heavily on human interpretation and experience to convert parameters into actionable insight. This paper presents the development of AUTUMN (Automated Tagging via Machine Learning & Natural Language Processing), a domain-specialized Large Language Model (LLM) designed to augment real-time drilling decision-making by synthesizing structured and unstructured operational knowledge into coherent, context-aware procedural reasoning. The LLM is fine-tuned using drilling-specific SOPs, SIDs, operational guidelines, After Action Reviews (AARs), and historical intervention datasets, enabling it to generate technically grounded recommendations aligned with institutional best practices and engineering standards. Through structured SME validation and scenario-based trials, AUTUMN demonstrates measurable improvements in the speed, consistency, and clarity of advisory generation. By reducing manual effort previously required for document retrieval and interpretation, the system allows MS to focus on higher-order analytical tasks and proactive risk management. The paper further outlines a scalable architecture designed for future integration with automated tagging application and anomaly-detection engines, enabling event-driven LLM triggering and end-to-end intelligent advisory workflows. Collectively, these capabilities illustrate the potential of domain-customized AI systems to fundamentally transform real-time decision support in complex drilling operations.

title: Are Multi-Agent Coding Frameworks Obsolete?
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
abstract: Episode summary: The "team of dev" AI frameworks promised to simulate an entire software company. But with models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet now capable of complex, native orchestration, are these multi-agent systems still relevant? We revisit MetaGPT, SWE-agent, and OpenHands to see if their architectural advantages—like SOPs, Agent-Computer Interfaces, and event-driven runtimes—still hold water in 2026. We explore the "Orchestration Tax" versus "Separation of Concerns," and give you a clear decision matrix for when to use a multi-agent framework versus a single, powerful model. Show Notes The promise of the "AI software company" was one of the most exciting concepts to emerge from the early days of large language models. Frameworks like MetaGPT, SWE-agent, and OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) aimed to move beyond simple chatbots and create autonomous engineering teams. But the landscape has shifted dramatically. With powerful models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet now featuring native tool use and orchestration, a central question has arisen: are these multi-agent frameworks still relevant, or have they been rendered obsolete by raw model power? This discussion explores the core architectural philosophies of these three major frameworks and evaluates their standing in the current ecosystem. The Case for Structure: MetaGPT and SOPs MetaGPT's foundational idea is that LLMs drift and hallucinate when faced with massive, open-ended tasks. Its solution is to enforce a rigid structure of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). Instead of a single prompt to "build an app," MetaGPT simulates a corporate workflow: a "Product Manager" agent writes a PRD, an "Architect" agent creates a system design, and only then does the "Engineer" agent write code. The key insight here is state management. Even with context windows exceeding 200,000 tokens, a model's "thinking" process can become muddled over a long conversation. By forcing the model to generate a PRD first, MetaGPT creates a persistent, structured memory that acts as a source of truth. This prevents the model from improvising a database schema in the middle of writing a UI component. It's a way to reduce the "temperature" of a project, keeping the model on a narrow track defined by its current role. While this feels like excessive paperwork for a small script, it provides invaluable guardrails for complex, multi-file repositories. The Interface Problem: SWE-agent's ACI SWE-agent tackles a different, more fundamental problem: the interface between the AI and the computer. Standard bash terminals are designed for humans who can scan hundreds of lines of logs and spot an error instantly. An LLM, however, sees the same output as a massive, confusing wall of tokens that consumes its context window. SWE-agent's solution is the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI). It replaces raw bash commands with specialized, structured commands like `search_dir`, `scroll`, and `edit_file`. When the model uses a `search` command, it doesn't get the noisy output of a standard `grep`; it receives a clean, truncated summary optimized for its reasoning. This is like giving the AI a pair of glasses instead of making it squint at a tiny screen. The result is a massive improvement in signal-to-noise ratio, which is why SWE-agent achieved high scores on benchmarks like SWE-bench. It's not necessarily that the underlying model was smarter, but that its "hands" were more precise. The Autonomous Colleague: OpenHands' Event-Driven Runtime OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) focuses on long-running autonomy and human oversight. Its recent move to an "event-driven runtime" is a game-changer for complex tasks. In a standard session, interaction is linear and blocking. If a task takes ten minutes to run, your terminal is tied up. OpenHands treats everything as an event in a sandboxed Docker container. An agent can trigger a long-running task, "detach" to work on something else, and react when the task completes. This mimics a real colleague who says, "I'll ping you when the migrations are done." More importantly, the sandbox provides a critical safety layer. If the agent decides to `rm -rf` something, it only destroys the container, not your actual machine. This safety allows for a level of autonomy that developers might hesitate to give a "naked" agent. Furthermore, OpenHands provides a visual dashboard where you can see the agent's thoughts and plans, pause it, edit its state, and steer it without a full restart—making it feel more like pair programming than prompting a script. The Orchestration Tax vs. Separation of Concerns A major counter-argument to multi-agent frameworks is the "Orchestration Tax." Every handoff between agents—like from Architect to Engineer—introduces a potential "translation error" where information is lost, like a game of telephone. If the Architect uses a term the Engineer interprets differently, the project can veer off course. However, the counter-argument is "Separation of Concerns." Even a brilliant model like Claude 3.7 can suffer from over-eagerness. When asked to architect and code simultaneously, it often rushes to write code because that's where the reward signal is in its training data. MetaGPT's SOPs act as a physical barrier, forcing a "Chain of Thought" at an organizational level. This structured handoff can be more reliable for a large project than hoping a single model remembers design patterns decided thousands of tokens earlier. The Decision Matrix: When to Use What So, when should a developer reach for a multi-agent framework? * **For a new, vague project:** Start with **MetaGPT**. Its strength is decomposition. It forces you to define user stories and data flows before writing code, acting as a senior lead that prevents scope creep from the AI itself. * **For navigating a massive, existing codebase:** Use **SWE-agent**. Its ACI is purpose-built for software engineering tasks, excelling at navigating large, unfamiliar file structures without getting lost. * **For long-running, complex tasks requiring human oversight:** Choose **OpenHands**. Its event-driven runtime and visual dashboard allow you to steer the AI, pause, and edit its plan, making it ideal for autonomous work that still needs a human in the loop. Ultimately, the choice isn't about which framework is "best," but which architectural advantage is most needed for the task at hand. The raw power of modern models doesn't make these frameworks obsolete; it just raises the bar for what they need to provide. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/multi-agent-coding-frameworks-2026

title: LSP: The Universal AI Coding Interface
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
abstract: Episode summary: The Language Server Protocol is evolving beyond static analysis to become the backbone of AI-assisted coding. This episode explores projects like lsp-ai and copilot-lsp-nvim, which leverage LSP's standard interface to bring generative models directly into the editor. Learn how this architectural shift promises to unify the developer experience, reduce plugin fatigue, and enable powerful new AI-driven features like context-aware refactoring and diagnostics. Show Notes A quiet architectural shift is underway in software development, moving the focus from the AI models themselves to the underlying plumbing that connects them to our tools. The Language Server Protocol (LSP), originally designed to standardize how code editors provide features like autocomplete and error checking, is now being repurposed as a universal interface for AI coding assistants. Originally introduced by Microsoft in 2016, LSP solved a major fragmentation problem. Before LSP, every editor—Vim, Emacs, Sublime Text—needed a custom plugin for every language to provide intelligent features. LSP decoupled the editor's user interface (the "client") from the language intelligence (the "server"). The editor handles the display of text and menus, while a separate server process handles parsing code, building syntax trees, and finding definitions. They communicate via a standard JSON-RPC protocol, usually over standard input/output. This standardization has created a perfect "slot" for AI. Projects like the open-source `lsp-ai` demonstrate this by implementing the standard LSP endpoints but connecting them to Large Language Models (LLMs) instead of traditional compiler backends. When an editor requests a code completion, `lsp-ai` doesn't analyze the syntax locally; it packages the relevant code context—potentially the entire file or project—and sends it to an LLM via an API or a local model. The editor receives a standard LSP response, completely unaware that the "intelligence" came from a generative model. This approach effectively bypasses the need for editor-specific AI plugins, allowing any LSP-compatible editor to gain AI capabilities instantly. The implications of this shift are significant. First, it unifies the developer workflow. Previously, developers often juggled a "dumb" editor and a separate "smart" AI chat window, leading to context-switching and copy-pasting. By embedding the AI directly into the LSP, the assistant becomes a native part of the editor's core nervous system. Features like "Code Actions" can be repurposed: a developer can highlight messy code, trigger a code action, and have the AI-LSP server refactor it into an idiomatic pattern, all within the familiar editor interface. Second, it enhances context awareness. Because LSP is already designed to understand project roots and file dependencies, an AI-powered server can leverage this structure. For instance, it can see a database schema defined in a SQL file and use that context to provide accurate completions in a Python ORM file, solving a common developer pain point. However, this integration isn't without friction. Traditional LSP servers are extremely fast, often responding in under 10 milliseconds. LLMs, even local ones, have a noticeable latency, which can disrupt the fluid feeling of editing. To mitigate this, tools like `lsp-ai` focus on local inference and optimized caching. The protocol itself supports asynchronous responses and partial results, helping manage user expectations by showing "thinking" status indicators in the editor's status bar. Another project, `copilot-lsp-nvim`, takes this a step further by wrapping the proprietary GitHub Copilot agent into a standard LSP server. This "meta-layer" approach allows editors that lack official Copilot plugin support to access its features simply by using a standard LSP client, further cementing LSP's role as the "HTTP of the editor world." This architectural move also offers a strategic advantage for privacy and flexibility. Developers and organizations can configure their AI-LSP server to use different models for different tasks—switching between a fast local model for completions and a powerful cloud model for complex refactoring—without being locked into a specific vendor's plugin. It represents a pro-consumer shift, decoupling the AI "brain" from the editor "eyes and hands." As long as the editor supports LSP, the AI capabilities can travel with the developer across different tools and environments. Ultimately, the repurposing of LSP for AI signifies a maturation of the AI coding toolchain. It moves beyond the novelty of chat-based assistants to a deeply integrated, context-aware, and editor-agnostic future. The protocol designed to help Microsoft compete with Java's IDE dominance has inadvertently become the foundational layer for the next era of software development. title: SDKs vs Raw APIs: The Developer's Real Choice
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: Ever wonder why companies like Stripe and Twilio invest so heavily in SDKs? This episode dives deep into the strategic difference between using a raw API and a software development kit. We explore how SDKs handle complex authentication, security compliance, and performance optimization that raw HTTP calls often miss. Learn why these tools are more than just convenience wrappers—they are a critical part of modern software architecture and developer experience. Tune in to understand the hidden costs of "rolling your own" integration and why an SDK might be the key to shipping faster and more securely. Show Notes When a developer needs to integrate a third-party service, they face a fundamental architectural choice: use a raw API or leverage a Software Development Kit (SDK). While a raw API offers direct control, this discussion reveals why SDKs are often the superior, strategic choice for modern applications. An API is simply a contract—a menu of available actions. An SDK, however, is the entire kitchen: a collection of pre-written libraries, documentation, and tools designed to implement a complete workflow around that API. One of the most compelling reasons to use an SDK is the massive reduction in complexity for critical tasks. Handling authentication, for instance, has become increasingly intricate with standards like OAuth 3 and complex token rotations. A well-built SDK manages this automatically, shielding the developer from the tedious and error-prone process of manually crafting authentication headers. Similarly, SDKs provide robust error handling and retry logic out of the box. Most developers writing a simple raw API call will implement a basic try-catch block, which fails the first time a network hiccup occurs. An SDK, by contrast, often includes sophisticated strategies like jittered exponential backoff, ensuring that temporary server issues don't crash an entire application. Beyond convenience, SDKs offer significant advantages in security and compliance. Companies like Stripe design their SDKs to be a "security shield." For example, the Stripe SDK handles PCI compliance by ensuring sensitive credit card data never touches the developer's server. Attempting this with a raw API would place a heavy security auditing burden on the developer. Furthermore, SDKs can integrate directly with secret management systems, solving the "Secret Zero" problem by communicating with an environment's identity provider instead of forcing developers to handle raw API keys that might be accidentally logged or leaked. Performance is another often-overlooked benefit. While some argue that abstraction layers add latency, a well-crafted SDK can actually be more performant than a series of raw HTTP calls. It can implement smart caching, reuse underlying TCP connections, and manage session states, reducing the overhead of constantly opening and closing connections. This is especially crucial when working with high-cost services like LLM APIs, where an SDK's efficient batching and caching can lead to direct savings on token usage and faster response times. From a strategic business perspective, companies invest heavily in SDKs to create a low-friction developer experience. The goal is to make their service the most invisible and reliable part of a developer's stack. By abstracting away carrier-specific quirks for services like Twilio or handling complex regional failovers for cloud providers like AWS, an SDK can reduce integration time from days to hours. This speed to market is a powerful competitive advantage. While this does create a form of vendor lock-in—making it harder to switch providers—it also offloads a significant maintenance burden. When a provider updates its API, they also update their SDK. The developer simply bumps a version number, and the "plumbing" code is handled for them. However, SDKs are not without their downsides. The primary concern is bloat, or "dependency soup," where a small library pulls in dozens of third-party dependencies, increasing bundle size and potentially introducing security vulnerabilities. A savvy development team must evaluate an SDK's dependency tree and favor modular designs that allow them to import only the necessary components. For teams concerned about vendor lock-in, a common best practice is to use a "service wrapper" or hexagonal architecture. This involves wrapping the vendor's SDK in an internal interface, providing the benefits of the SDK while keeping the option open to switch providers by only changing the code within that wrapper. Ultimately, the choice isn't just about convenience; it's about drawing the line of abstraction. In an unreliable network environment, drawing that line inside the application logic with an SDK is often the safer, more robust choice. title: Hybrid Governance Architecture: A Self-Improving Memory Substrate for LLM Agents with Progressive Cost Reduction and Deterministic Replay
authors: Ahmet Yiğit Sertel
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Title Hybrid Governance Architecture: A Self-Improving Memory Substrate for LLM Agents with Progressive Cost Reduction and Deterministic Replay Authors Ahmet Yiğit Sertel (Independent Researcher, İzmir, Turkey) ORCID: 0009-0003-4959-7004 Description Large language model agents pay the same inference cost for every query, regardless of how many times they have encountered the same pattern. Dense retrieval-augmented generation mitigates context limitations but does nothing to reduce the underlying token expenditure. We present the Hybrid Governance Architecture (HGA), a three-layer memory substrate that separates semantic retrieval, exact recall, and decision replay under a unified governance gate. HGA routes each incoming query to the cheapest execution path that can handle it correctly: novel queries invoke full LLM reasoning; familiar, validated patterns replay deterministically without any LLM call. The architecture comprises three layers. L1 (Routing Memory) provides VQ-compressed semantic retrieval with 768× index compression. L2 (Deterministic Vault) guarantees 100% exact recall for structured facts via SHA-256-verified key-value storage. L3 (Semantic Neuron Layer) learns and replays tool-calling decisions through a four-stage maturation protocol. A governance gate fuses four signals — confidence, margin, sensitivity, and neuron maturity — to select among five execution paths ranging from full LLM reasoning (~131 tokens) to deterministic replay (~5 tokens) to zero-cost exact lookup. Across 14 experiments, two of which use a live GPT-5.4-nano API: 89.5% token savings over 1,000 episodes (end-to-end integration); 78.1% token savings over 400 real API queries vs. Dense-RAG baseline; 100% deterministic consistency on Stage 3 replays (vs. 79% for the LLM); zero silent failures across 300 adversarial and out-of-distribution probes; 94% phase-weighted gate accuracy with 0% unsafe fast-path rate; 768× routing index compression (100 KB vs. 76.8 MB for 100K items); 38.6% memory reduction via salience-guided forgetting with 100% recall preservation. The system requires no external dependencies beyond SQLite, works with any LLM provider and embedding model, and is fully modular — L1 operates standalone as a retrieval engine, L3 can be disabled for non-agentic deployments. The core mechanism is vector quantization repurposed as a semantic routing primitive: the same VQ codebook that compresses the retrieval index also provides the signals that drive execution path selection, making HGA less a memory system than a learned execution router that progressively shifts reasoning cost from the LLM to validated, deterministic replay. All 14 experiments are reproducible. The paper includes complete methodology, gate pseudocode (Algorithm 1), scalability projections, per-path latency and memory footprint analysis, and an honest assessment of limitations including workload dependence, statistical power constraints, and transfer boundaries. Keywords LLM agents; memory architecture; vector quantization; decision replay; cost optimization; deterministic execution; governance gate; semantic routing; retrieval-augmented generation; neuron maturation Resource Type Preprint License Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Related Identifiers Sertel, A. Y. (2026). Routing Memory: VQ-Based Semantic Retrieval with 768× Index Compression. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19241718 (is supplemented by this upload) Subjects Computer Science — Artificial Intelligence Computer Science — Machine Learning Computer Science — Software Engineering Additional Notes Experiment data includes 12 simulated experiments (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, K=256 codebook) and 2 live API experiments (GPT-5.4-nano via OpenAI API). The experiment suite was redesigned from scratch after identifying validity problems in the original design; the current suite uses real embeddings and gate-independent ground truth throughout.

title: Research on an Intelligent Review Process for High-Level Requirements of Avionics Software Based on Large Language Models
authors: Yige Zhao; Zichun Yi; Jinghua Sun; Yajun He; Siqi Wu
abstract: The review of avionics software High-Level Requirements (HLRs) is a critical engineering activity required to comply with airworthiness standards such as DO-178C and ARP4754B, and the quality of this review directly affects the safety and consistency of subsequent design, implementation, and verification processes. However, traditional manual review approaches are time-consuming, labor-intensive, highly dependent on reviewer experience, and often lack consistency. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-based HLR review method. The proposed approach explicitly models requirement review criteria and adopts a multi-stage review workflow with customized prompt engineering, effectively constraining LLM behavior and improving the accuracy of requirement analysis. In addition, a systematic evaluation and optimization scheme for LLMassisted avionics software HLR review is introduced to provide structured guidance for subsequent end-to-end development and to continuously improve review accuracy. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly reduces manual review effort, improves defect detection rates, and outperforms traditional manual review in semantic consistency checking and global logical analysis, thereby confirming its feasibility and practical value in avionics software engineering.

title: Improving Software Testing with RAG-Based LLMs and Supporting Indian Regional Languages
authors: Carol Joanna Bright M; Kripaa P; Karishma S; Freida Judith I; Usama Rahman
abstract: Automated generation of software test cases are one of the crucial tasks in modern software engineering, while the traditional method of manually writing test cases is time-consuming, prone to making errors and often fails to achieve contextual or linguistic accuracy. This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation based method, which integrates dynamic knowledge retrieval with LLMs to generate highly faithful and contextually grounded test cases. Unlike general fine-tuned LLMs, which require extensive retraining, the proposed RAG pipeline uses lanceDB to store domain related knowledge and SentenceTransformers to semantically retrieve knowledge from the database, thus offering more reliability with much lower computational cost. Besides this, the suggested pipeline allows multilingual test case generation done by the LLM model across English and other Indian regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada making software test more inclusive for language sensitive software ecosystems. The generated test cases are observed to be semantically aligned with the retrieved context and real-world user stories thus improving factual consistency and software reliability. Experimental evaluation shows consistent faithfulness scores, showing the effectiveness of the RAG pipeline and LLMs generation. Results confirm the embeddings quality, retrieval accuracy and reasoning capability within the model. Also, the architecture can be optionally extended for user feedback-based continual learning by integrating it with QA platforms such as Jira via Model Context Protocol (MCP) which gives the possibility to modify the model as per the project requirements. Overall, this study shows that RAG based models could provide scalable, multilingual and intelligent automation in future software quality assurance.

title: Understanding Developer Responses to Agent-Generated Code Review Comments
authors: Anonymous Author(s)
abstract: Code review is a critical quality assurance practice in software engineering development, and AI coding agents are increasingly generating review comments on pull requests. However, little is known about how developers actually respond to such agent-generated feedback. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study on the resolution of agent-generated code review comments. We analyze $54{,}713$ comments generated by three widely used coding agents (i.e., Copilot, Cursor, and Codex) across $341$ Python repositories on GitHub. We examine (1) resolution rates across agents and comment types, (2) the role of developer experience, and (3) characteristics that influence comment usefulness. Our results show that resolution rate varies considerably across agents, with Copilot accounting for the majority of resolved comments (72.9\%). Core developers resolve the majority of agent-generated feedback, particularly for \textit{design} and \textit{evolvability}-related comments, while peripheral developers are more involved in resolving \textit{functional defect} comments. Through open card sorting of 470 unresolved comment discussions, we identify \textit{ten} discussion patterns explaining why comments remain unresolved, with \textit{incorrect suggestions} and \textit{intentional design decisions} being the most prevalent. Finally, our analysis reveals that the presence of an inline \textit{code suggestion} is the strongest predictor of comment usefulness, while providing rules, examples, and benefit-based explanations also modestly increase the likelihood of adoption. Our findings provide insights for improving agent-generated code review feedback and its integration into development workflows.

title: Replication package for “Go Home Copilot, You’re Drunk”: Understanding Developer Responses to Agent-Generated Code Review Comments
authors: Anonymous Author(s)
abstract: Code review is a critical quality assurance practice in software engineering development, and AI coding agents are increasingly generating review comments on pull requests. However, little is known about how developers actually respond to such agent-generated feedback. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study on the resolution of agent-generated code review comments. We analyze $54{,}713$ comments generated by three widely used coding agents (i.e., Copilot, Cursor, and Codex) across $341$ Python repositories on GitHub. We examine (1) resolution rates across agents and comment types, (2) the role of developer experience, and (3) characteristics that influence comment usefulness. Our results show that resolution rate varies considerably across agents, with Copilot accounting for the majority of resolved comments (72.9\%). Core developers resolve the majority of agent-generated feedback, particularly for \textit{design} and \textit{evolvability}-related comments, while peripheral developers are more involved in resolving \textit{functional defect} comments. Through open card sorting of 470 unresolved comment discussions, we identify \textit{ten} discussion patterns explaining why comments remain unresolved, with \textit{incorrect suggestions} and \textit{intentional design decisions} being the most prevalent. Finally, our analysis reveals that the presence of an inline \textit{code suggestion} is the strongest predictor of comment usefulness, while providing rules, examples, and benefit-based explanations also modestly increase the likelihood of adoption. Our findings provide insights for improving agent-generated code review feedback and its integration into development workflows.

title: LLM inference delay prediction based on machine learning algorithms
authors: Jingtao Zhang; Haorui Gao
abstract: Large language model technology is evolving rapidly, with the number of parameters increasing from billions to hundreds of billions. Its applications cover areas such as intelligent dialogue, code generation, and academic writing. However, inference latency is gradually becoming the core bottleneck restricting its industrial deployment. The interaction of different model configurations, hardware performance and other factors leads to significant fluctuations in latency. For instance, the inference latency of a model with hundreds of billions of parameters on the CPU can reach the second level. Under high concurrency, it can also cause problems such as a decline in user experience and waste of computing power. However, machine learning algorithms, with their data-driven characteristics, have become the key to solving the problem of latency prediction. To break through the limitations of existing algorithms in the collaborative modeling of global and temporal features, the research first conducted correlation analysis and violin graph analysis, and then through comparative experiments of multiple machine learning algorithms, it was found that The DE-Transformer-BiLSTM algorithm is generally superior to multiple algorithms such as ExtraTrees and Random Forest in terms of prediction performance. Only some error indicators are slightly inferior to DE-Transformer-BiLSTM, and the goodness of fit is even better. Its design that integrates kernel extreme learning machines, long short-term memory networks and Transformer architecture enables it to surpass traditional algorithms in terms of feature extraction and time series prediction accuracy. This algorithm provides an effective path for the precise prediction of LLM inference latency, which can help optimize the allocation of computing power resources and improve user experience, laying an important technical foundation for promoting the industrial deployment of LLM.

title: The Impact of LLMs on Software Development
authors: Shadurceya Vasanthakumar; Ruwan Wickramarachchi
abstract: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in software development has raised expectations regarding improved productivity, code quality, and development efficiency. However, empirical evidence on their impact across different stages of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) remains limited. This study examines how software professionals use LLMs in practice and the benefits and limitations of their use. The study combines a systematic review of 75 peer-reviewed studies with survey data from 207 software professionals, supported by semi-structured interviews. LLM usage was examined across eight software engineering outcome areas, including Productivity and Efficiency, Code Quality and Reliability, Security and Vulnerability Management, Governance, Ethics and Trust, Client Experience and Satisfaction, Communication and Collaboration, Job and Role Transformation, Innovation and Creativity. The findings indicate perceived improvements in productivity, innovation, and professional role transformation alongside a substantial impact on security and vulnerability management practices. In the security domain, LLMs influence vulnerability identification and remediation while also introducing new security risks and biases. In contrast, no clear improvements were reported in code quality, client satisfaction, or team collaboration. These findings suggest that current benefits are largely confined to individual workflows, while broader system-level outcomes remain less affected. This study offers empirical, multi-dimensional insights evidence to inform future integration strategies emphasizing structured adoption, enhanced quality assurance, and collaborative development practices.

title: A Hybrid LLM-Driven Recommendation System for Selecting Flutter Packages Using Structured Metadata and Stack Overflow Knowledge
authors: R. M. I. M. Bandara; K. G. L. Chathumini; B.T.G.S. Kumara
abstract: The rapid growth of the Flutter ecosystem has created significant challenges for developers when selecting appropriate third-party packages, particularly in complex categories such as state management. Existing selection approaches typically rely on individual metrics such as popularity or download counts, which fail to capture contextual aspects of developer intent, real-world problem discussions, or semantic alignment between user requirements and package capabilities. To address this limitation, this paper presents a hybrid recommendation system that integrates structured metadata from official Flutter repositories with unstructured community knowledge extracted from Stack Overflow. The system employs large language models (LLMs) to interpret natural-language user queries, extract relevant technical attributes, and compute semantic relevance across multiple data sources. Three LLMs-GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-were comparatively evaluated to assess their effectiveness in technical intent extraction and semantic matching. GPT-4-Turbo was selected as the primary inference engine based on its superior accuracy, consistency, and resistance to hallucinations. The final recommendation model applies a weighted scoring mechanism that integrates popularity, recency, likes, downloads, accepted answers, sentiment signals, and LLM-based semantic relevance to produce ranked package recommendations aligned with developer requirements. This approach ensures that recommendations incorporate both quantitative repository indicators and qualitative developer experiences. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves high precision, recall, and semantic matching accuracy across multiple evaluation scenarios. Expert validation further confirms that the generated recommendations align with real-world development practices and demonstrate the practical value of the system. Although the study focuses on Flutter state-management packages, the proposed methodology can be generalised to other categories within the Flutter ecosystem. The findings highlight the potential of hybrid LLM-assisted frameworks to improve developer decision-making and enhance the efficiency of package selection in modern software engineering environments.

title: AI Enhanced Code Fault Detection and Automated Fixing
authors: V Arun Antony; T.A.Karthikeyen; N.Kannan; S.Gowtham; V. Jai Akash
abstract: Software development can be characterized by complex programs, which can carry with them, syntactic errors and logical bugs, therefore debugging becomes a very time consuming and a demanding undertaking. Conventional debugging systems are intensive in their utilisation of manual effort and rule-based tools which have some limitations in identifying run-time problems and supplying automatic solutions. We present a new AI-based automated debugging system in this paper that combines dynamic validation and pre-trained large language models with a static code analysis to detect bugs and code fixes efficiently. The system makes use of parsing based on Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to retrieve the functional level components, create test cases, and also detect possible errors as well as logical inconsistency. Pretrained models include CodeLlama, Mistral 7B, CodeT5, and StarCoder which are used to produce context-aware fixes, and a memory module based on vectors is used to increase efficiency by retrieving similar patterns of past bug-fixes. The system is based on an iterative validation procedure to provide accuracy on generated solutions. The experimental analysis based on similarity-based measurements proves that CodeLlama has the best mark of 91.2, which reflects the competence of the offered method in automated program repair and code optimization assignments.

title: Greening AI-Assisted Code Generation by Reducing Babbling
authors: Anonymous Anonymous
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the implementation and experimental artifacts for our study on babbling in Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation. Babbling refers to unnecessary or excessive output produced by LLMs, which can increase cognitive load, energy consumption, and operational costs. We introduce Babbling Suppression (BS), a simple, model-agnostic method that integrates test execution into the generation process. BS evaluates intermediate outputs and terminates generation as soon as a solution passes all predefined tests, preventing unnecessary token generation without compromising accuracy. Our empirical evaluation spans Python (HumanEval and MBPP) and Java(HumanEval Java and APPS) benchmarks and 10 models of 3B–7B parameters. Repository Structure The following models are used in the study: CodeLlama-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, Deepseek-6.7B, CodeGemma-7B, CodeQwen1.5-7B, NextCoder-7B, Phi3.5-4B, Phi4-4B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-3B-Coder-Instruct. The following benchmarks are used: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval Java(referred to as MULTI-PL), and APPS. The raw data, containing energy readings and token timestamps, is stored for all ten models in the same structure as presented below. Folders: Results CodeLlama-7B/: experiments that were conducted using this model. HumanEval/: contains raw data obtained from running baseline or BS for HumanEval. Baseline: the choice of the method used for code generation. *_energy_measurement.txt: raw power readings with timestamps using pynvml. *_inference_time.txt: timestamps for each token generation. Jupyter Notebooks: BabblingSuppressionJava.ipynb: contains implementation for BS for Java, loads and runs all models for chosen benchmark and method (Baseline or BS). BabblingSuppressionPython.ipynb: contains implementation for BS for Python, loads and runs all models for chosen benchmark and method (Baseline or BS). CheckJavaAccuracy.ipynb: evaluates accuracy of the generated results for one of the Java benchmarks. CheckPythonAccuracy.ipynb: evaluates accuracy of the generated results for one of the Python benchmarks. DataAnalysis.ipynb: processes raw measurements for a selected model, benchmark and method, and reports benchmark-averaged metrics including total inference energy, output length, and energy per token. QuantifyingBabblingJava.ipynb: produces the plots of Figure 1b from the paper, that show which tokens are part of the correct solution and where babbling appears. QuantifyingBabblingPython: produces the plots of Figure 1a from the paper, that show which tokens are part of the correct solution and where babbling appears. A jar file is in the jars folder and is already integrated in the BS. APPS: dataset.json is in the APPS folder. title: The Governance of Human Capacity in the AI Age, Vol. 3: Toward a Multi-Level Doctrine of AI Use — From Foundational Theory to Personal Cognitive Governance
authors: Xiangyu Guo
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Governance of Human Capacity in the AI Age, Vol. 3: Toward a Multi-Level Doctrine of AI Use — From Foundational Theory to Personal Cognitive GovernanceCivilization Physics — Human Systems & AI Integration Series This paper develops a multi-level doctrine of AI use, arguing that effective and sustainable integration of generative AI is fundamentally a governance problem rather than a purely technical or productivity problem. As AI expands the executable surface of work—producing drafts, code, plans, and alternatives at low marginal cost—the limiting factor shifts to the capacity to supervise, verify, integrate, and take responsibility for those outputs. This shift reflects a well-established pattern in automation: when execution is absorbed by machines, human roles become more cognitively demanding and more consequential. The analysis begins by identifying the structural pressures introduced by generative AI. Empirical evidence shows measurable productivity gains across domains such as customer support, writing, and software development. However, these gains coexist with increased demands for oversight and verification due to the probabilistic nature of AI outputs, including hallucinations and subtle errors. At the same time, the emergence of agentic workflows and tool-augmented systems expands the operational surface that must be governed, introducing new requirements for logging, access control, provenance, and auditability. To address these dynamics, the paper proposes a four-level doctrine framework, organizing AI use across distinct but interconnected layers: Foundational theory — establishes shared assumptions about AI behavior, uncertainty, and the persistence of human accountability. Industry doctrine — translates these assumptions into sector-specific norms, including acceptable error tolerances, verification standards, and disclosure practices. Organizational workflow — operationalizes governance through roles, processes, artifacts, and metrics that integrate AI into production systems. Personal cognitive governance — defines how individuals manage attention, task switching, trust calibration, and decision-making under AI-assisted conditions. This layered structure ensures that responsibility is distributed appropriately across systems, institutions, and individuals, rather than being reduced to isolated practices such as prompt engineering. The paper identifies several structural constraints that make such a doctrine necessary. Automation paradoxes show that increased automation can intensify human supervisory burdens and reduce readiness to intervene during failures. Cognitive limits, including restricted working memory and task-switching costs, impose hard ceilings on how much parallel AI-generated activity a person can reliably manage. LLM behavioral characteristics, such as fluent but potentially incorrect outputs, require continuous verification and framing. Together, these constraints define a condition in which capability expands faster than governance capacity. A key contribution of the paper is the formalization of governance as a multi-level system requirement. At the foundational level, AI outputs must be treated as probabilistic proposals rather than authoritative facts. At the industry level, norms must standardize verification and accountability practices. At the organizational level, workflows must separate generation, verification, integration, and sign-off functions, supported by testing, evaluation, validation, and verification processes. At the personal level, individuals must adopt practices that preserve cognitive bandwidth, including option budgeting, structured work cycles, externalized decision tracking, and explicit stopping rules. The paper further introduces a social governance dimension of AI use. Because AI systems are optimized for low-friction interaction—fast, always available, and socially costless—they can displace human consultation and informal knowledge exchange. This creates a structural risk: the erosion of relational infrastructure through which expertise, judgment, and shared standards are maintained. The paper argues that governance must explicitly preserve human consultation pathways in contexts involving ambiguity, risk, or shared accountability. Empirical evidence and institutional guidance reinforce the framework. Studies show productivity gains alongside cognitive and motivational trade-offs, including reduced critical thinking effort and altered engagement patterns. Professional and regulatory bodies in law and medicine explicitly reaffirm human responsibility and verification obligations. International governance frameworks emphasize risk management, lifecycle oversight, and continuous monitoring, aligning with the doctrine’s emphasis on scalable governance capacity. The paper concludes that the central challenge of the AI era is not maximizing capability, but aligning capability with governance capacity. Systems that expand execution without expanding oversight, verification, and accountability risk instability, degraded decision quality, and erosion of trust. Within the Civilization Physics framework, this work establishes a general principle: sustainable AI use requires layered governance structures that preserve human judgment, cognitive integrity, and institutional responsibility as capability scales. Keywords: AI Governance · Cognitive Load · Human-AI Interaction · Automation Paradox · Multi-Level Doctrine · Cognitive Offloading · Trust Calibration · Organizational Design · Risk Management · Civilization Physics

title: Claude Code: Engineering with the Agentic Harness
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
abstract: Episode summary: In this episode, we dive into the rapid evolution of AI-driven development, where 4% of all GitHub commits are now fully authored by autonomous agents. We explore the technical architecture of Claude Code's "agentic harness," a system that provides the reasoning power of Claude Opus 4.6 with the tools, file access, and execution environment necessary to function as a senior developer. From the mechanics of the agentic loop—context gathering, execution, and verification—to the security implications of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), we break down how these systems are tripling autonomous problem-solving capabilities. We also discuss the shift toward asynchronous workflows with Claude Code Channels and the rise of Agent Teams, where multiple sub-agents collaborate under a single architect. Whether you're interested in the massive productivity gains reported by Anthropic or the security risks of internet-exposed MCP servers, this episode provides a comprehensive look at the state of AI engineering in 2026. Show Notes The landscape of software engineering has shifted fundamentally. As of early 2026, four percent of all public GitHub commits are authored entirely by artificial intelligence agents. This isn't just a rise in autocomplete suggestions; it represents a move toward fully autonomous systems that write, test, and commit code. At the center of this shift is the concept of the "agentic harness," a specialized wrapper that transforms a Large Language Model (LLM) from a passive observer into an active participant in the software development lifecycle. ### The Architecture of the Harness A standalone LLM is essentially a stateless prediction engine—a "brain in a jar" with no direct access to a file system or terminal. The agentic harness provides the "biological equivalents" necessary for work: a hard drive, a terminal, and the ability to manage state. By using a harness, the model can run bash commands, interpret error outputs, and engage in recursive reasoning loops without human intervention. The core of this system is the agentic loop, which consists of three phases: context gathering, execution, and verification. During context gathering, the agent traverses the directory and reads project-specific rulebooks like `CLAUDE.md`. In the execution phase, it uses tool-use capabilities to modify files. Finally, in the verification phase, it runs test suites and linters. If a test fails, the agent treats that failure as new input and restarts the loop until the problem is solved. ### Reasoning and Integration Modern agents like Claude Opus 4.6 utilize a "thinking budget," allowing for extended reasoning tokens. This architecture enables the agent to plan complex architectural changes and simulate outcomes before touching the disk. This internal chain of thought is visible to the developer, building trust through transparency. Integration is handled via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standardized adapter that allows the agent to connect to external tools like Jira, Slack, or SQL databases. While MCP bridges the gap between code and business logic, it introduces new security challenges. Recent reports indicate thousands of internet-exposed MCP servers lack proper authorization, creating significant vulnerabilities in zero-trust environments. ### The Shift to Asynchronous Workflows The relationship between developer and AI is moving from synchronous chatting to asynchronous partnership. New features like "Channels" allow developers to assign a multi-hour refactoring task to an agent in the terminal, close their laptop, and receive a notification on a mobile device once the job is complete. Furthermore, the rise of "Agent Teams" allows a single session to spawn sub-agents. These sub-agents work in parallel on different parts of a codebase—such as backend logic and frontend components—while a parent "architect" agent ensures consistency across the project. ### Conclusion The transition to agentic workflows is yielding massive productivity gains, with some organizations reporting that AI now handles 60% of daily engineering tasks. For developers, success in this new era depends on curating persistent project "brains" through markdown-based memory files, ensuring the agent retains the specific intuitions and standards of the local codebase. The following sections outline the scientific consensus and theoretical underpinnings that validate this approach. 1. Centaurian System Architectures The protocol aligns with the paradigm of "Centaurian Systems" recently formalized in system theory.
