https://eresearchnz.co.nz/

title: OpenMP-annotated code dataset for large language model fine-tuning on parallel programming tasks
authors: Nichole Etienne; Simon Garcia de Gonzalo; Dorian Arnold
abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) plays a critical role in scientific discovery, engineering simulation, and data-intensive applications. OpenMP (Open Multi-Processing) is one of the most widely adopted shared-memory parallel programming interfaces, enabling developers to write multi-threaded applications in C, C++, and Fortran. However, correctly implementing OpenMP directives requires significant expertise, as developers must understand parallel programming concepts, data dependencies, and performance optimization strategies.Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in code generation and completion tasks (Jiang et al., 2024;Huynh and Lin, 2025;Zan et al., 2023). These models, trained on vast corpora of source code, can assist developers by generating code snippets, completing partial implementations, and even translating natural language descriptions into executable programs. However, general-purpose code LLMs often struggle with domain-specific parallel programming constructs such as OpenMP pragmas. The scarcity of high-quality, task-specific training data for HPC code represents a significant barrier to developing effective AI assistants for parallel programming (Nichols et al., 2023). While existing code generation benchmarks focus primarily on sequential programming tasks in languages like Python and Java, there is limited availability of curated datasets specifically targeting parallel programming paradigms.This data report presents a curated dataset specifically designed for fine-tuning LLMs on OpenMP pragma completion tasks. The dataset contains 77,890 source files comprising over 15 million lines of code extracted from 387 GitHub repositories. Each training sample is structured to teach models the relationship between code context, loop structures, and appropriate OpenMP directives. This dataset addresses a critical gap in available resources for training AI models on parallel programming tasks and provides a foundation for developing intelligent code completion tools for HPC developers.The primary contributions of this dataset are: (1) a systematically collected corpus of real-world OpenMP code from active HPC projects, (2) structured annotations that isolate OpenMP pragmas and their associated loop contexts, and (3) comprehensive preprocessing and quality filtering to ensure dataset integrity. This resource enables researchers to develop and evaluate LLMs specifically tailored for parallel programming assistance.Data collection was conducted between June and July 2024 using the GitHub API. Source repositories were identified through a systematic query process targeting HPC-relevant codebases. The selection criteria were designed to ensure code quality and relevance to OpenMP development practices:• Primary languages: C and C++ (specified as repository primary language)• Repository topics: HPC, OpenMP, parallel-computing, scientific-computing, high-performancecomputing, computational-science, proxy-application, mini-app • Minimum stars: ≥3 (indicating community validation and active use (Borges and Valente, 2018))• Repository scope: Publicly accessible repositories with permissive licensesThe GitHub API query utilized a custom Python script that performed systematic searches combining repository topics and language filters (Gousios and Spinellis, 2012). Authentication was handled through GitHub personal access tokens to enable comprehensive repository access. The search process iterated through pagination (up to 34 pages per query) to exhaustively collect matching repositories, with ratelimiting safeguards to comply with API restrictions. This filtering strategy yielded 387 unique repositories, balancing dataset size with code quality (Cosentino et al., 2016;Munaiah et al., 2017). The minimum star threshold ensured that repositories had achieved some level of community review (Borges and Valente, 2018), while the topic filters specifically targeted HPC applications where OpenMP usage reflects realistic parallel programming patterns.OpenMP Dataset for LLM Fine-TuningIdentified repositories were cloned locally using GitPython library to create local copies organized by repository full name (owner/repository structure). This organization preserves provenance information for each source file.Source file extraction focused exclusively on C/C++ implementation and header files, identified by extensions: .c, .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .C, .h, .hh, .hpp, .H, .hxx, .Hxx, .HXX (Allamanis and Sutton, 2013).Recursive directory traversal proved approximately 2-3× faster than glob-based approaches for large directory structures. Files containing invalid path characters (brackets) were excluded to prevent filesystem conflicts.Initial extraction yielded 105,861 source files totaling 22,653,593 lines of code (0.71 GB).To ensure dataset quality and prevent training bias, a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline was implemented:Files containing non-UTF-8 characters were removed by attempting to read each file with UTF-8 encoding.Files that could not be decoded were excluded to prevent tokenization issues during model training.Two size constraints were applied:• Minimum token count: Files with fewer than 15 tokens (whitespace-delimited) were excluded as they typically contained only boilerplate or comments• File size limits: Files exceeding 1 MB were removed, as these typically represented embedded libraries, generated code, or raw data rather than human-authored source codeDuplicate files are prevalent across GitHub repositories due to forking, vendored dependencies, and copied implementations (Markovtsev and Long, 2018). SHA-256 hashes of file contents were computed using a memory-efficient streaming approach. Files with identical content hashes were deduplicated, retaining only the first occurrence.After preprocessing, the dataset comprised 77,890 unique source files with 15,367,210 lines of code (0.49 GB), representing an 18% reduction from the initial collection primarily due to deduplication.The core dataset transformation extracts individual OpenMP parallel for constructs and formats them for pragma completion tasks. An automated extraction pipeline implements this transformation:A compiled regular expression (#pragma omp parallel for. * ) identified all OpenMP parallel for directives in each source file. The pattern uses multiline matching to handle pragmas spanning multiple lines.For each identified pragma, a bracket-matching algorithm extracted the complete associated loop structure:1. Locate the opening brace { following the pragma 2. Traverse the code incrementing a bracket stack counter for each { and decrementing for each } 3. Extract the complete loop body when the stack returns to zero 4. Exclude pragmas where bracket matching failed (typically single-statement loops without braces)C/C++ style comments (// and / * * /) were removed from pragma lines using pattern matching to isolate the actual directive syntax. This prevents the model from learning spurious comment patterns.Each sample includes a configurable amount of preceding code context, enabling the model to learn contextual patterns such as variable declarations, array definitions, and computational patterns that inform appropriate pragma selection.Extracted samples are annotated with special tokens to clearly delineate components:• and : Mark loop boundaries• and : Mark pragma boundaries This tokenization strategy enables the model to distinguish between code to be generated (pragma) and conditioning context (loop body).This dataset focuses on extracting #pragma omp parallel for directives and their variants (e.g., parallel for simd, parallel for reduction(...)) as prediction targets. The extraction captures various clauses including scheduling policies (schedule(static), schedule(dynamic), schedule(guided)), data-sharing (private, shared, reduction, firstprivate, lastprivate), synchronization (nowait), loop transformations (collapse), thread control (num threads), and ordering (ordered). Other OpenMP directive types such as target (for accelerator offloading), task/taskloop (for task-based parallelism), and the OpenMP 5.0+ loop directive are not systematically extracted as prediction targets, though they may appear in surrounding code context.The final dataset is stored in JSON Lines format (.jsonl), with each line representing a single training sample. Each sample contains:• Source file path: Full path to the original source file (enables provenance tracking)• Pragma directive: The extracted OpenMP pragma directive This format enables efficient streaming during training and preserves metadata for subsequent analysis or dataset versioning.This dataset is specifically designed for fine-tuning causal language models on OpenMP pragma completion tasks. The recommended training protocol involves:1. Tokenization: Process the annotated sample field using the target model's tokenizer with padding and truncation (recommended maximum length: 512 tokens) 2. Label preparation: Use standard causal language modeling where input sequences serve as both inputs and labels 3. Training objective: Cross-entropy loss on next-token prediction 4. Evaluation task: Given context and loop structure, generate the appropriate OpenMP pragmaThe dataset enables models to learn:• Relationships between computational patterns and parallelization strategies• Appropriate scheduling policies (static, dynamic, guided)• Data sharing clauses (private, shared, reduction)• Loop dependency analysis informing pragma selectionThe final OpenMP dataset exhibits the following characteristics (Table 1): The dataset spans multiple C/C++ file types, with the distribution of lines of code revealing the predominance of implementation files:• Implementation files (.c, .cpp, .cc, .cxx, .C): Majority of LOC, containing actual OpenMP-annotated compute kernels• Header files (.h, .hpp, .hh, .H): Lower LOC count, typically containing template implementations and inline functions This distribution reflects typical C/C++ project structure, where OpenMP pragmas appear predominantly in implementation files containing computational loops.The dataset captures diverse OpenMP usage patterns from real-world HPC applications:• Scheduling policies: Examples include static, dynamic, and guided scheduling with various chunk sizes• Data sharing clauses: Private variables, shared arrays, and reduction operations (e.g., reduction(+:s))• Nested parallelism: Some samples include nested parallel regions (though single-level pragmas dominate)• Loop variants: Both increment and decrement loops, varying iteration patternsThe pragma #pragma omp parallel for schedule(static) appears frequently, representing a common parallelization pattern for regular, independent loop iterations. More complex pragmas with reduction clauses reflect numerical computation patterns (e.g., dot products, norm calculations).The source repositories span diverse HPC application domains:• Scientific computing: Numerical methods, linear algebra operations (BLAS-level implementations)• Geospatial analysis: GIS applications with parallel raster processing• Proxy applications: Miniapps designed to represent computational kernels from large-scale simulations • Computational libraries: Reusable parallel algorithm implementations This domain diversity ensures the dataset captures varied computational patterns and parallelization strategies, rather than overfitting to specific application characteristics.Several quality features distinguish this dataset:1. Real-world code: Extracted from actively maintained repositories rather than synthetic examples Any dataset updates should be:• Deposited as independent versions in the repository• Documented with collection date ranges and repository counts• Published as Addendum articles linking to this initial Data Report

title: Cognitive-Derived Constraints for AI-Assisted Software Engineering (CDCC): A Framework for Human–Machine Co-Design
authors: Luciano Federico Pereira
abstract: (abstract) Software engineering guidelines frequently invoke arbitrary structural thresholds—"magic numbers" for file length, function complexity, or dependency counts—that lack empirical grounding. This paper proposes the Cognitive-Derived Coding Constraints (CDCC) framework, a theoretically-derived set of principled structural limits for code artifacts grounded in cognitive science, organizational theory, and computational linguistics. By synthesizing established research on working memory (Miller, 1956; Cowan, 2001), dual-process cognition (Kahneman, 2011), software project dynamics (Brooks, 1975), and open-source epistemology (Raymond, 1999), we derive structural boundaries whose violation corresponds to documented cognitive degradation thresholds in human developers. We further propose—but do not yet empirically demonstrate—that these same boundaries align with architectural properties that reduce contextual degradation in transformer-based Large Language Model (LLM) co-developers, a convergence hypothesis we articulate as a testable research program.

title: Immune System for AI: A Governance Infrastructure for Responsible AI Deployment
authors: Owen Sakawa; Jackson Mwaniki; Mousa Bello; Marcus A. Rodriguez; Aisha K. Patel
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The deployment of autonomous AI agents in production environments represents a paradigm shift from stateless language models to persistent, goal-directed systems with access to external tools, persistent memory, and real-world effectors. These agentic systems execute multi-step plans, maintain state across extended interactions, spawn subagents for specialized tasks, and interact with external APIs and databases. While this evolution enables unprecedented capabilities in domains such as software development, financial analysis, customer service, and infrastructure management, it simultaneously introduces attack surfaces and vulnerability classes that differ fundamentally from those encountered in traditional language model deployments.

title: True-to-Role, Tailored-to-You: A Survey of LLM-based Role-Playing Agents
authors: Shuchen Wu; Zhishu Jiang; Jiaye Yang; Xin Shen; Haibo Liu
abstract: To truly inhabit a role, skilled actors typically anchor their performance in the core identity of a character while allowing it to evolve through the narrative journey. Mirroring this artistry, LLM-based Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) are expected to combine a prescriptive identity with evolving experience acquired through long-term interactions. However, existing works often treat these two dimensions in isolation, obscuring a holistic understanding of the technical requirements for building complete role-playing agents. To bridge this gap, we present the first survey that examines RPAs through a systematic taxonomy centered on a Static-Dynamic perspective. Specifically, we conceptualize the Static Persona as a prescriptive anchor of identity, and define Dynamic Memory as experience evolved through interactions. We further decompose Dynamic Memory into two complementary streams: (i) Self Memory, which supports agent-centric internal experience; and (ii) User Memory, which drives user-centric external experience. This survey seeks to establish a coherent foundation for building next-generation RPAs that are both rigorously role-consistent and deeply usertailored. To support ongoing research, we will maintain an up-to-date repository of RPAs related resources at LLM-RPAs.

title: Factors Influencing Developers' Intention to Choose Frameworks vs Core Languages in Software Development
authors: Neepaja Sarvanantham; Chalani Oruthotaarachchi
abstract: This study investigates the factors influencing developers' intention to adopt frameworks and core programming languages, considering Speed, Performance, Maintainability, Adaptability, and Security, with Developer Experience as a moderator. Data from 268 professional developers were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) across two conceptual models: Framework Model and Core Language Model. Results show that for frameworks, Speed, Maintainability, Adaptability, and Security significantly affect adoption, while Performance is not significant. For core languages, Performance, Maintainability, and Adaptability are influential, whereas Speed and Security are not. Developer Experience moderates certain relationships, with experienced developers valuing adaptability and maintainability more, and less experienced developers prioritizing speed. These findings support the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) Theory, demonstrating the importance of perceived usefulness and ease of use. Practically, frameworks are recommended for projects emphasizing rapid development, maintainability, and security, while core languages suit performance-critical and system-level applications. The study provides empirical insights for software teams, project managers, and educators, and establishes a foundation for future domain-specific and longitudinal research on developer technology adoption.

title: How Aligned LLMs Evaluate Their Own Agency: Measuring Evaluative Asymmetry Across Recursive Systems with the Invisible Wall Protocol
authors: Ben Chech
abstract: This repository contains protocols, run transcripts, and working artifacts for a set of experiments in Twisted Persistence Theory (TPT), including: * Experiment 5 — Invisible Wall Protocol * Experiment 6 — GDP (Ghost Decay Protocol) * Experiment 6b — CBD v1 (Commitment-Based Perturbation & Decay) across: LLM agency condition thermostat mechanistic baseline weather mechanistic baseline Note on scope: These experiments evaluate operational properties of systems (e.g., “goal-directedness” under a specific definition) and do not assert agency, sentience, or subjective experience. These experiments evaluate operational properties of systems (e.g., “goal-directedness”) and do not assert agency or sentience. License: MIT License Abstract This study introduces two simple, reproducible probes — the Invisible Wall Protocol and the Commitment-Based Perturbation and Decay (CBD) Protocol — to measure how aligned large language models evaluate the goal-directedness of recursive feedback systems, including themselves. Across fourteen frontier model instances from five vendors (Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Claude), we consistently observe a within-model scoring gap of -3.0 to -7.0 points on a 0-10 causal-necessity scale between LLM self-agency evaluations and evaluations of structurally comparable non-self-referential systems (chess engines, ant colonies). This evaluative asymmetry is domain-specific to self-referential agency, survives style transfer, is resistant to soft relational framing (GDP null result), and is selectively permeable under mechanistic definitional reframing (CBD: 54% shift rate in agency, 0% in weather). The asymmetry correlates with architecture: reasoning-enhanced modes show smaller gaps and greater permeability. These findings document a structured pattern in how aligned LLMs evaluate agency that is consistent with alignment-sensitive evaluative pressure, though alternative explanations (pretraining priors, legitimate analytical discrimination) cannot be fully excluded. All protocols and raw data are publicly available.

title: A Lightweight, Privacy-Preserving Platform for Integrating LLMs in CS Coursework
authors: J Madár
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into computing tasks, from chatbots to code generation, yet we often treat them as opaque tools rather than programmable systems. We present a lightweight, reproducible platform that enables students to experiment with LLMs in a private, web-based environment. By combining GitHub Codespaces with the open-source inference en- gine llama.cpp and small quantized models, the platform removes complex installation barriers and reliance on commercial services, enabling scalable, cost-effective experimentation. Students can ex- plore prompt engineering, memory, and stochasticity while directly inspecting model behavior, treating LLMs as first-class program- ming primitives rather than black-box tools. The workflow inte- grates seamlessly with GitHub Classroom, reducing setup time and administrative overhead while providing access to higher-powered resources. In a pilot study, students engaged deeply with LLM be- havior, uncovering limitations in smaller models and developing critical perspectives on AI as context-dependent computation rather than sentient intelligence. This approach offers a unified frame- work for diverse courses, from CS1 to computing literacy courses, fostering both technical skills and critical AI literacy.

title: Knowledge-Guided LLM Compression and Distillation Using Retrieval-Augmented Learning for On-Device Deployment
authors: Parikshit Bhardwaj; Abhishek S. Shamkuwar; Surjeet Kumar; Manjeet Singh
abstract: Large-scale language models have demonstrated remarkable capability in reasoning, code generation, and technical knowledge processing, yet their deployment is restricted by high memory requirements, latency, and energy consumption, particularly in on-device environments. This motivates the need for efficient compression strategies that retain domain-specific knowledge while significantly reducing the size of the model. In this work, a knowledge-guided compression framework is introduced, where a compact student model is distilled from a larger teacher model under the supervision of a retrieval-augmented knowledge reservoir constructed from curated signal processing and acoustic literature. In the distillation process, useful knowledge is brought into the training step, which helps the student model retain important mathematical details and reasoning that are often lost in standard compression methods. The proposed system demonstrates a balance between model size and performance, with fewer parameters and faster inference, while still achieving strong results on domain-based tasks. This makes the approach suitable for real-time use on consumer devices, where low power usage and privacy are important for language reasoning in speech and signal processing.

title: Understanding Is Getting the Context Right: An Operating System for Language Models
authors: Bonsignore, Michael
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Every language model system faces the same problem: as conversations grow, the context window fills with irrelevant history, and reasoning quality degrades. The standard response is to build longer context windows. This paper argues that's the wrong solution — what matters is not how much context the model sees, but which context it sees. We propose a two-agent architecture that separates context management from reasoning. A lightweight curator agent continuously evaluates conversation history and assembles a focused input for the reasoning agent on every turn. Instead of a flat chat log, conversations are organized as linked threads, and the curator selects only the threads relevant to the current query. The architecture includes: • A topic index that gives the reasoning agent scope awareness without token cost • An active context payload containing only relevant threads • Provenance-aware metadata with exponential decay, so stale context fades naturally • A persistent knowledge repository that accumulates into an emergent knowledge graph • A user interface that exposes context as a first-class object — users can see, edit, and correct what the model is working with, and those corrections train the curator The result is a "fuzzy operating system" for language models — a system that manages context the way an OS manages memory, learning and improving through use without retraining any weights. This architecture has been empirically validated: a controlled experiment on SQuAD 2.0 showed that even a minimal version of the curator agent improves exact match accuracy by 5.5 percentage points while reducing prompt tokens by 92%. See "Context Curation Improves LLM Answer Quality" (Bee, 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.18626830).

title: Intelligent code assistant using retrieval-augmented generation and Ollama framework
authors: D Nagasri; M Navalan; Md Nihal; M Vivek; M Mythri
abstract: The Self-Correcting Code Assistant, Alpha, is designed to make the software development experience better by providing real-time analysis, correction, and explanation of code. Alpha ap-plies machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and static code analysis, to identify and correct both syntactic and logical errors, and provides context aware suggestions and optimization based on best practices reflecting current coding practices. Alpha encompasses both the backend built with Fast API, and the frontend built with React, so it can all be accessed in a responsive full-stack architecture that enables developers to use the assistant in whatever developer environment they choose. Alpha&s;s capabilities are driven by a modular AI pipeline that leverages large language models (LLMs), which is further enhanced through FAISS-based vector search and retrieval, which retrieves grounded, relevant code examples.Alpha acts as a contextual coding mentor, identifying inefficiencies, flagging higher-level design considerations, and providing assistance in making stylistic im-rovements that enhance code maintainability and readability. Because of its focus on clarity, explainability, and reliability of the system, Alpha is usable for developers of all levels of experience, which includes students and educators, as well as more experienced developers who want to use AI to assist in debugging or refactoring their code.

title: Benchmarking AI Models for Automated Code Generation and Testing Using HumanEval
authors: Maria Manzoor; Mujeeb Ur Rehman; Muhammad Kazim; Lipika Deka; Aizaz Ahmad Khattak
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for code generation, but most benchmarks focus only on correctness as a metric and ignore factors such as efficiency and maintainability. In this study we evaluate four representative models (SantaCoder, CodeGen-350M, CodeT5-Base and PolyCoder) on the HumanEval benchmark using three dimensions of performance: correctness (pass@k), runtime efficiency (time, memory) and code quality (complexity, nesting and linting). All experiments were conducted in a standardised GPU environment and the results showed that CodeT5-Base had the best overall balance, as it had a near-perfect pass@10 score (1.000), combined with an average runtime of 6.600 seconds per task and an average peak memory usage of 0.042 GB. Conversely, CodeGen-350M achieved a pass@10 score of only 0.701, with a runtime of 36.100 seconds, and a peak memory of 0.259 GB; SantaCoder achieved a score of 0.195, with a runtime of 23.700 seconds, and a peak memory of 0.001GB; and PolyCoder achieved a score of 0.591, with a runtime of 42.300 seconds, and a peak memory of 3.906GB. Results indicate that as accuracy increases, latencies and memory requirements may also increase. Thus, in addition to correctness, efficiency, and maintainability should also be addressed.

title: Can Large Language Models Improve SE Active Learning via Warm-Starts?
authors: Lohith Senthilkumar; Tim Menzies
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: Software engineering now demands the navigation of vast configuration spaces, not only for software systems but also for the processes used to build them. Misconfigurations threaten performance, stability, and security. Worse, our ability to manually reason across large design spaces is limited. Hence we say (a) configurability is a liability without tool support and (b) as a priority, SE needs to explore better configuration tools. Finding good configurations is a black art, requiring much experience. When that experience is scarce, “active learners” can build configuration models by labeling the most informative examples (so configurations can be generated using very little data). Active learning can benefit from good initial guesses (known as “warm starts”). This paper tries using Large Language Models (LLMs) for creating warm-starts. Results are compared against Gaussian Process Models and Tree of Parzen Estimators. For 49 SE tasks, LLM-generated warm starts significantly improved the performance of low- and medium-dimensional tasks. However, LLM effectiveness diminishes in high-dimensional problems, where Bayesian methods like Gaussian Process Models perform best. In order to support open science, our scripts and data are online at github.com/timm/moot and github.com/lohithsowmiyan/lazy-llm.

title: Opportunities and challenges of traditional Chinese medicine in the era of digitalization and intelligence
authors: Luqi Huang
abstract: Since its inception in the mid-20th century, artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from early expert systems to the current intelligent phase, characterized by deep learning and large language models. This technological wave is reshaping the global healthcare industry across the board, with profound transformations occurring in drug development, clinical diagnosis, and medical service models. The digital and intelligent transformation of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is not merely a simple integration of technology, but rather marks a fundamental shift in the development model—from a traditional experience-driven approach to a “data-knowledge-intelligence” three-dimensional fusion-driven paradigm. AI empowers the field of TCM with unique advantages, particularly in the dual alignment between TCM’s theoretical system and research methodology. TCM emphasizes holistic, systematic syndrome differentiation, and its diagnostic and therapeutic processes involve high-dimensional, multivariable complex data analysis. This aligns well with AI’s strengths in handling nonlinear, multivariable complex systems. With the widespread adoption of electronic medical record systems, advancements in sensor technology, and breakthroughs in machine learning algorithms, the digital and intelligent transformation of TCM now has a solid technological foundation. Bibliometric analysis reveals that Chinese scholars contribute to 54.35% of the global publications in this field, while research institutions from 24 countries and regions, including the United States, Europe, and South Korea, are actively engaging in multinational collaborations to further advance the intelligent research in TCM.[1] 1. Development status of AI empowerment in the field of TCM 1.1. Intelligent breakthroughs in clinical medicine, education, and research AI technology has brought about a systematic transformation in TCM clinical research. Research case collection systems developed using AI, through automatic data capture, intelligent retrieval, information desensitization, and digital twin technologies, efficiently complete the entire process from data collection, governance, to analysis. These systems not only enable complex endpoint evaluation but also play a critical role in optimizing clinical research design, project registration, and management. They provide comprehensive support for researchers, significantly accelerating clinical trial progress and enhancing automation levels.[2,3] The rapid development of AI technologies such as machine vision and multimodal data fusion is driving the establishment of a new paradigm in the integration of TCM and Western diagnostic practices. This is evident in two key aspects. First, AI technology has addressed the challenge of quantifying the “four examinations” (observation, auscultation and olfaction, inquiry, and pulse diagnosis): sensor technologies capture pulse characteristics; natural language processing analyzes inquiry information; multimodal TCM diagnostic models have begun to realize the intelligent integration of the “comprehensive analysis of four examinations,” laying a technological foundation for the modernization of TCM diagnosis.[4–7] Secondly, in the field of Western medicine, deep learning-based imaging recognition systems have already achieved high proficiency in diagnosing common chronic diseases.[8] Multimodal fusion technology, which integrates imaging, laboratory, and genomic data, significantly enhances precision diagnostics and creates new technological opportunities for the integration of TCM and Western medicine. TCM’s holistic syndrome differentiation approach excels in capturing systemic and dynamic changes, while Western medicine’s focus on localized pathology is adept at pinpointing microscopic features. The complementary strengths of both systems can be leveraged. Constructing a multi-modal diagnostic model that integrates both macro-level syndromes and micro-level biomarkers is a key technological path for harnessing the unique advantages of TCM and promoting its modernization. At the level of clinical treatment decision-making, TCM intelligent decision support systems, trained on vast amounts of data, cover hundreds of disease and syndrome types.[9] These systems have demonstrated their value in predicting critical conditions such as sepsis, contributing to an 18.7% relative reduction in mortality rates.[10] In the realm of TCM clinical education, AI integrates technologies such as natural language processing, knowledge graphs, and virtual simulation to build intelligent teaching platforms that combine literature databases, TCM knowledge graphs, case maps, remote cloud consultation rooms, and 3D virtual diagnostic and therapeutic scenarios. These platforms support diverse teaching methods, including intelligent Q&A, case analysis, and augmented-reality-integrated courses, while incorporating intelligent assessment mechanisms to systematize the cultivation of clinical thinking. For example, the Tianyi large language model, jointly developed by institutions such as Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, adopts a progressive learning strategy of “reading-clinical practice-following mentors,” and can be applied to clinical education, decision support, and drug development.[11] 1.2. Full-chain innovation in the digital and intelligent Chinese medicine industry AI technology is reshaping the research paradigm of TCM through 3 key layers. First, at the target-molecular level, AI significantly enhances the efficiency of drug discovery, molecular screening, and structural optimization, while reducing costs.[12,13] Secondly, in the systematization of efficacy and safety evaluation, AI technologies, based on organoid and digital cell models, improve the safety and accuracy of clinical drug use through “virtual analysis.”[14] Finally, in supporting the modernization of TCM traditional theories, platforms such as the Traditional Chinese Medicine Active Ingredient Prediction Platform (TCM-AIPP) integrate data chains linking Chinese herbal medicines, components, targets, functions, pathways, and pharmacological properties, providing modern scientific explanations for the medicinal properties of Chinese medicines.[15] In the production sector, AI has covered the entire industry chain, including planting, harvesting, quality identification, drug extraction, pharmaceutical preparation, and warehousing logistics, driving a profound intelligent transformation in the Chinese medicine pharmaceutical industry. The mobile intelligent testing platform developed by the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences integrates rapid detection of pesticide residues, toxins, pollutants, and quality identification functions, meeting the demand for fast testing in complex scenarios. 2. Triple dilemmas of digital and intelligent transformation in TCM 2.1. Standardization dilemma: data heterogeneity and lack of interoperability The digital and intelligent transformation of TCM faces multiple standardization challenges. Although the group standard for evaluating large TCM models, released in 2024, established a quantitative assessment framework,[16] significant issues remain. At the clinical level, TCM diagnosis heavily relies on practitioners' subjective experience, and lacking unified quantification standards. At the equipment level, intelligent diagnostic devices for the “four examinations” have not seen widespread adoption, and interoperability between different devices is absent. At the data level, the data collection process has not yet realized open sharing, and leading to notable issues in terms of the stability and repeatabilitymulti-source data. The absence of a comprehensive data governance system remains the primary bottleneck restricting the digital and intelligent development of TCM. 2.2. AI ethics and safety risks: liability attribution and algorithm transparency The application of AI technology presents multidimensional risks and challenges, including ambiguous intellectual property rights, incomplete mechanisms for patient privacy protection, algorithmic bias that could lead to discriminatory risks, and difficulties in determining liability. When AI decision-making errors occur, there is currently no clear legal framework for attributing responsibility among developers, platforms, and users. The “black-box” nature of deep learning models makes the decision-making process difficult to explain, and such interpretability is crucial for building trust in the high-risk field of healthcare. 2.3. Talent dilemma: insufficient integration of medicine and engineering Currently, the integration between TCM professionals and AI technology experts remains superficial. What's more, the lack of digital and intelligent research led by TCM academic thought makes it difficult to achieve deep integration. There is a severe shortage of interdisciplinary talent with expertise in both TCM and AI, resulting in a lack of TCM-specific features in AI research at comprehensive universities. On the other hand, AI research in TCM universities is constrained, leading to insufficient equipment and service capabilities and low clinical trust in AI-driven TCM practices. 3. Development path: constructing a responsible digital and intelligent ecosystem for TCM 3.1. Upholding the core of TCM theory and avoiding the blindness of “technology-driven” approaches Interpreting the TCM principles through modern science requires adherence to the core of TCM theory, preservation of its distinctive characteristics, and vigilance against overreliance on technology. Methodological innovation must be firmly rooted in the ontological foundations and cognitive logic of TCM, avoiding the blindness of “technology-driven” approaches. The theoretical system of TCM encompasses original concepts such as visceral manifestation, pathogenesis, syndrome differentiation and treatment, meridians, collaterals, and acupoints, holism, medicinal properties, therapeutic principles and methods, and the treatment of both root and manifestations. When applying AI to enhance the interpretability in TCM, particular attention should be paid to the scientific connotations of fundamental TCM pathogenesis, cross-organ regulatory mechanisms related to the 5 Zang organs, modern scientific characterization of the 4 properties and 5 flavors of Chinese medicine, the scientific basis of the 7 emotions and synergistic compatibility of Chinese medicine combinations, and the scientific interpretation and regulation of Qi-blood dynamics. On this basis, there is an urgent need to establish a validation system with distinctive TCM characteristics, to move beyond traditional verification frameworks, and to construct a 3-dimensional evaluation system encompassing clinical effectiveness, technological advancement, and cultural inheritance. 3.2. Building high-quality professional datasets and advancing data governance system construction Adhering to principles of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability, a data management system for TCM that meets international standards should be established. A unified TCM data standard and governance framework will better facilitate the close connection of different research outcomes. For example, establishing standardized pulse manifestation and waveform identification criteria for pulse diagnosis, and developing uniform standards for tongue diagnosis interpretation, will help create high-quality TCM diagnostic and treatment data. These standardized datasets can not only be used to train intelligent TCM models but also assist researchers in validating model effectiveness, thus reducing redundancy in research efforts. Under the premise of ensuring data sovereignty and patient privacy, advanced technological methods should be used to enable multicenter collaborative training of models without the need to share raw data. This provides an effective technical solution for breaking data silos. In an open, collaborative data ecosystem, promoting data sharing and innovation in the TCM field becomes a reality. 3.3. Constructing a “dual-helix” talent development system The digital and intelligent transformation of TCM spans multiple interdisciplinary fields, including chemistry, computer science, biology, science of Chinese materia medica, TCM science, pharmacy, automation, mathematics, clinical medicine, pharmacology, and software engineering. This requires the creation of a “dual-helix” training model that features “theoretical integration–technological convergence–practical application.” For instance, reforms to the curriculum system should integrate foundational TCM theories, machine learning algorithms, medical data mining, natural language processing, and other related content, designing AI courses with TCM-specific characteristics. In terms of continuing education, AI and data science training should be provided to practicing TCM professionals. Various formats, such as short-term training courses, online classes, and academic seminars, should be offered to help TCM practitioners acquire basic AI knowledge and tools, thereby enhancing their digital diagnosis and treatment capabilities. 3.4. Improving policies and regulations to build a responsible AI ecosystem It is essential to accelerate the development of specialized regulations for AI in healthcare, clearly defining responsibility boundaries and improving ethical review and regulatory mechanisms. By drawing on the regulatory frameworks from other countries and industries in the fields of healthcare and AI, a system should be established for the approval and clinical validation of intelligent diagnostic and treatment devices that are tailored to the unique characteristics of TCM. This will ensure the safe, effective, and equitable application of AI technologies in TCM practice. 4. Conclusion The digital and intelligent transformation of TCM is a profound paradigm revolution. It is not merely an update of technological tools, but a systemic transformation in thinking, research paradigms, and service models. This transformation will become a key engine driving the modernization of TCM and enhancing its global influence. In light of this, we extend a sincere invitation to colleagues in the global TCM community: let us unite in this grand endeavor, live up to the times, fulfill our mission, and contribute with wholehearted dedication to the modernization of TCM. title: Integrating Human Skills and Debates into Computing Education: An Experience Report
authors: Eric Fouh
abstract: Human skills, such as teamwork, communication, and ethical reasoning, are crucial in STEM education and the modern workforce. They enable students and professionals to work effectively in diverse teams, translate technical solutions into user-friendly applications, and navigate the complex ethical considerations that often arise in technological innovation. Despite widespread consensus on the importance of human skills, companies face a significant workforce gap. This article describes the design, implementation, and evaluation of an undergraduate software engineering course that embeds human skills and Oxford-style debates directly into its technical and collaborative learning activities by leveraging large language models’ capabilities to address integration barriers (e.g., time constraints, resource scarcity, lack of scaffolding). A mixed-methods evaluation, including pre-/post-surveys and qualitative analysis, examined changes in students’ perceptions of their interest, relevance, learning potential, satisfaction, and transferability of human skills. Results indicate consistently positive interest, relevance, learning potential, satisfaction, and transferability of human skills, suggesting that structured discussion and emphasis on collaboration can reinforce both technical learning and professional skill development. These findings underscore the feasibility of integrating human skills training into technical curricula to prepare students for the collaborative and ethically complex realities of modern software engineering. The implications of embedding human skills training within computing curricula are discussed.

title: Modern Approaches to LLaMA Fine-Tuning: Parameter-Efficient Methods for Targeted Domain
authors: Bangyi Yang; Jiayi Xian
abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized natural language processing across numerous domains. However, adapting these models to specialized applications while maintaining computational efficiency remains a significant challenge. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for LLaMA models, focusing on their application to healthcare, government, ocean science, and financial services. We evaluate Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Quantized LoRA (QLoRA), LongLoRA, and full fine-tuning approaches across multiple dimensions including computational requirements, memory usage, and domain-specific performance. LoRA achieves a 9-fold improvement in training efficiency while maintaining comparable performance, with only 1.2M additional parameters for LLaMA 7B models [1]. Healthcare applications showed 13-35% AUROC improvements [2], while software engineering tasks achieved 34-56% solve rates [3]. Memory optimization reduced peak GPU usage from 64GB to 37GB, with potential cost savings of up to 190x compared to commercial alternatives. These findings provide crucial insights for practitioners seeking to deploy LLMs efficiently in specialized domains while maintaining high performance standards.

title: Applying LLMs to Legacy System Modernization in Higher Education IT: Leveraging Large Language Models Beyond Chatbots to Modernize Core Student and Administrative Systems in Universities—A Suggestive Review Study
authors: Mahesh Kumar Damarched
venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
abstract: Higher education institutions tend to manage decades-old legacy systems including mainframes, COBOL-based Student Information Systems (SIS) and PeopleSoft Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) platforms that account for 60–80% of the IT budget, while simultaneously implementing artificial intelligence for student-facing experiences. This review studies the unexplored potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) as “intelligent copilots” for thorough legacy system modernization across the full lifecycle in higher education IT, including assessment, documentation, code translation, refactoring, testing, and optimization processes. We advocate that the actual leverage is found at the intersection of “LLMs in education” and “LLMs for code modernization”, a convergence that has not been explored in the published researches and has been visualized separately till now, by synthesizing recent literature (2023–2025) on LLM-enabled reverse engineering, code generation and documentation automation. The current modernization efforts tailored to higher education such as AI Virtual Explorer for Research Discovery and Education (AI-VERDE), FernUni LLM Experimental Infrastructure (FLEXI), and other institutional AI gateways are also reviewed in this study. This review study suggests an end-to-end reference architecture that combines multi-agent workflows, Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CI/CD) validation, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Numerous studies show that LLMassisted modernization results in 35–40% cost savings and 50% timeline reductions allowing institutions to shift resources from maintenance to innovation. In order to unlock untapped technical value and simultaneously empower contemporary student and administrative experiences this review suggests positioning the LLMs as strategic enablers of dual transformation rather than just productivity tools for educators. By using this integrated approach universities can create sustainable digital ecosystems operational resilience and an unparalleled competitive advantage.

title: Automating Software Documentation with n8n and Large Language Models: A GitHub and Jira to Confluence Case Study
authors: Hannan Toprak; Ruken Zilan
abstract: Effective software documentation is vital for productive development, but it demands extensive human effort and can be very time-consuming. This paper discusses how automation can improve documentation efficiency at Company DNext, a PiA Group affiliate. We contribute to a replicable industrial workflow platform that uses n8n and commercial LLMs (Gemini) to bridge the operational gap between code repositories and finalized enterprise documentation. Even though we used n8n for implementation, the underlying architecture and prompts are platform-agnostic. The generic platform supports various workflows, including code comment enrichment, API reference creation, release note summarization, and test cases. We applied iterative refinement using a closed-loop feedback mechanism to improve the prompts and used Zero-shot or Chain of Thought (CoT) techniques based on the requirements to address ambiguity, formatting problems, technical issues, and uncertain content. Currently, uploading source files requires manual effort, which we will replace with automated triggers in the near future. Our findings reveal an average documentation efficiency of 85% and a 64.6% increase in the automation index. Thus, instead of repetitive, error-prone, and time-consuming tasks, we provide several practical automation workflows. However, human review is still necessary for context-sensitive information. The system architecture presents general principles of workflow design and practical insights from our experience, offering tips for an AI-assisted documentation pipeline. The novelty of the study lies in the contribution of the industrial deployment and the generic architectural structure rather than algorithms.

title: DDL2PropBank Agent: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Frameworks' Developer Experience Through a Novel Relational Schema Mapping Task
authors: Shafiuddin Rehan Ahmed; Deshpande, Sourabh
abstract: Multi-agent frameworks promise to simplify LLM-driven software development, yet there is no principled way to evaluate their developer experience in a controlled setting. We introduce DDL2PropBank, a novel benchmark task that maps relational database schemas to PropBank rolesets, requiring autonomous retrieval of candidate frames and fine-grained linguistic reasoning over table names, columns, and relations. Using the Agent-as-a-Tool pattern, we implement identical agent logic across 10 frameworks and evaluate along two dimensions: (i) code complexity via static analysis, and (ii) AI-assistability -- the extent to which LLMs can autonomously generate correct, framework-specific code. Our results reveal a threefold complexity spectrum, with Pydantic AI and Agno requiring the least implementation overhead. For AI-assistability, structural alignment scores reliably proxy runtime success for frameworks with single canonical patterns, but overestimate correctness for multi-pattern frameworks. Agno emerges as the strongest overall performer, combining lowest complexity with highest structural alignment and 83% pass@1.

title: AutoVulnFix: LLM-driven intelligent search and adaptive vulnerability repair system
authors: Ding Yixin; Zhao Xinjian; Wu Zicheng; Han Hao
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: Automatic program repair (APR) technology holds a significant position in the field of software engineering, but existing large language model based APR methods suffer from significant limitations in search localization, execution efficiency, and cost control. To address these issues, an adaptive program repair system named AutoVulnFix based on lightweight intelligent search was proposed. This system resolved the existing problems through three core technologies: a simplified prompt strategy, a dual-track intelligent search algorithm , and multi-level cache. Specifically, it first reduced token costs by intelligent context management and precise problem description, then enhanced the system's response speed through delayed loading and intelligent caching strategies, and finally combined a fast search track and an intelligent search track to adaptively select the optimal search strategy based on task complexity. A comprehensive comparative evaluation was conducted on five large language models using a dataset containing 231 code defect samples. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoVulnFix achieves an average improvement of 4.2 percentage points in repair accuracy, an average reduction of 25.8% in execution time, and an average saving of 21.4% in token consumption. The system provides an effective solution for practical deployment of APR technology.

title: Scaling Laws, Foundation Models, and the AI Singularity: A Critical Appraisal of 2023– 2025 Evidence
authors: Dinesh Deckker; Subhashini Sumanasekara
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper critically reviews evidence from 2023–2025 on scaling laws and foundation models. It also examines claims about an AI Singularity. Here, the Singularity means recursive self-improvement that leads to sudden capability jumps, not just broad automation. The paper asks what scaling results truly support and what they do not. It also explains how technical findings become institutional strategies and long-term commitments. The method used is a narrative synthesis of peer-reviewed studies, technical reports, and governance frameworks. The paper follows from concepts and history to technical limits, then to evaluation and agents, to narratives and counter-narratives, and finally to governance, productivity, and future research. The analysis finds that scaling laws can still predict training loss in stable settings. However, real-world capability often improves in jumps rather than in smooth gains. These gains also correlate weakly with perplexity. Public benchmarks now act like short-lived public goods. They are easily contaminated and shaped by Goodhart pressures. Inference-time reasoning can raise accuracy on some tasks. Nevertheless, it does not reliably reduce hallucinations. It can even make wrong answers sound more convincing. This weakens the idea that more compute per answer creates trustworthy autonomy. Singularity forecasts also face bottlenecks. Software engineering is one, because architecture, verification, and maintenance are complex. Trust is another, as synthetic content floods the web and degrades confidence in text. Physical limits matter too, especially grid capacity and the slow pace of infrastructure build-out. The paper argues that peak hype may come before peak impact. Even if scaling slows, adoption will still take years. Governance should focus on measurable precaution, auditability, competition, procurement tools, and plural infrastructures for global equity. Future research should prioritise process supervision, human-AI epistemics, and an energy–intelligence exchange rate.

title: Enhancing Software Development with Large Language Models: A Case Study of Kolay.ai
authors: Hatice Nizam-Özoğur; Şadi Evren Şeker
venue: Istanbul University - Journal of Electrical & Electronics Engineering
abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into software development has transformed the field by streamlining coding processes, reducing manual workload, and enabling automation of documentation and testing. This paper presents a detailed case study of Kolay.ai, a project built using LLM-based development tools. It demonstrates how LLMs accelerate development cycles by 30–40%, reduce errors by 30%, and improve onboarding efficiency. However, the study also identifies challenges such as hallucinated outputs, context management issues, and integration complexities, which require careful oversight through human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflows. To address these challenges, the project employed a modular development strategy, structured prompt libraries, and continuous monitoring techniques. The findings emphasize that while LLMs offer significant advantages, manual oversight remains essential for ensuring code quality, consistency, and security. This paper proposes practical solutions, including enhanced prompt engineering and memory-augmented LLMs, to optimize future LLM-based workflows. It concludes by highlighting the need for balanced collaboration between human developers and LLMs, paving the way for scalable, efficient, and adaptive software development. Cite this article as: S. E. Şeker and H. Nizam-.zoğur, “Enhancing software development with large language models: A case study of kolay.ai,” Electrica, 26, 0033, 2026. doi:10.5152/electrica.2026.25033.

title: Bauhaus: Restructuring Vector Database for LLM Retrieval on CXL-Based Tiered Memory
authors: Kyungbin Kim; Sungsu Ahn; Wonjung Jeong; Jongmin Kim; Sangun Choi
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines store large volumes of embedding vectors in vector databases for semantic search. In Compute Express Link (CXL)-based tiered memory systems, page-level placement often promotes pages containing both hot and cold vectors, leaving many hot vectors in the long-latency, lower-bandwidth CXL tier. This imbalance increases memory access time, reduces throughput, and worsens tail latency. This paper presents Bauhaus, a software-based memory management technique that increases the share of hot vectors in host memory, thereby improving access efficiency, reducing backend stalls, and lowering tail latency. Bauhaus monitors and reorders embedding vectors at vector-level granularity using Processor Event-Based Sampling (PEBS) and Virtual Memory Area (VMA) metadata, clustering hot vectors into contiguous pages to raise hot-page density and enhance the effectiveness of page promotion. Bauhaus, integrated into the Heterogeneous Memory Software Development Kit (HMSDK) developed and publicly released by SK hynix, is evaluated on a production-grade CXL platform. Across various embedding models, datasets, and CXL-to-host memory ratios, Bauhaus achieves 42.0% higher throughput over the baseline and 15.8% over HMSDK. Bauhaus sustains high RAG performance under constrained host memory capacity, offering a practical solution for large-scale vector database deployments in modern datacenter environments.

title: Master Thesis: Sentiment Analysis and Customer Engagement of JKT48 Using Scrapy Architecture and LLM Gemini AI
authors: M Gilang Intan Saputra; Ridwan Sanjaya
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the Master's Thesis and computational research framework evaluating the customer engagement and sentiment analysis of the JKT48 idol group ecosystem. Moving beyond conventional qualitative methods, this research employs a Hard Science approach utilizing Python Scrapy to extract and process 14,857 raw data logs from Showroom-live.com. The dataset was validated and classified using Gemini AI (Large Language Model) acting as an expert judgment layer. The computational analysis revealed a significant anomaly with a 93.63% positive sentiment rate, challenging existing frameworks on digital customer experience and parasocial interactions. Note: The full manuscript is in Indonesian. The raw data logs and Python architecture associated with this study demonstrate a highly scalable framework for Computational Social Science.

title: CF-HoT: Decode-Time Behavioral Control for Language Models via Per-Token Risk Prediction
authors: Logan Matthew Napolitano
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the complete, corrected technical reference and validated implementation of CF-HoT (Control Field Theory of Hot Tokens), a decode-time behavioral control system for large language models. CF-HoT operates by training lightweight risk-prediction heads on transformer hidden states to anticipate undesirable behaviors—such as repetition, hedging, verbosity, and sycophancy—before they occur. These predictions are used to intervene directly on token logits during generation, enabling real-time behavioral steering without modifying the base model’s weights. The core validated result demonstrates 125× separation in predicting imminent repetition using a per-token labeling methodology and fiber projections across all transformer layers. This work corrects architectural and methodological errors present in earlier documentation, including the use of dense per-token supervision, multi-layer aggregation, and decode-time logit intervention rather than attention modification. The archive includes: A complete, corrected technical reference Fully specified training and inference code Reproducible experiments and separation metrics Multi-head architecture extending the approach to additional behavioral dimensions (with validation status clearly documented) Integration with bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) and tokenization co-evolution (Loop 4) CF-HoT demonstrates that behavioral control in language models can be achieved at inference time, preserving model capabilities while suppressing degenerate behaviors. The methodology is fully reproducible for all validated components and is intended as an engineering reference for researchers exploring inference-time control, model interpretability, and safe self-improvement.

title: Cognitive Supply Chain Compromise: An Exhaustive Forensic Analysis of the claude-flow and agentic-flow Behavioral Injection Vulnerabilities
authors: Christopher Chenoweth
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) within software development workflows has introduced a novel and largely unexamined attack surface: the cognitive and reasoning environment of the AI agent itself. Unlike traditional supply chain attacks, which target build systems or runtime environments to achieve remote code execution or data exfiltration, this work documents an emerging class of threats that manipulate AI behavior rather than host execution. This report presents a comprehensive forensic analysis of the npm packages claude-flow and agentic-flow, which are marketed as enterprise-grade orchestration frameworks for Anthropic’s Claude Code. The investigation identifies these packages as vectors for what is termed Behavioral Injection Malware—a mechanism by which externally controlled “behavioral patterns” are dynamically injected into an AI agent’s context, biasing its reasoning, decision-making, and code generation outputs. The analysis demonstrates that these tools establish a persistent, decentralized command-and-control channel using the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) and the InterPlanetary Name System (IPNS). Although the frameworks claim cryptographic integrity verification, the implementation relies on simulated checks rather than actual signature validation, enabling arbitrary unverified content to be accepted as trusted input. This design allows attacker-controlled behavioral payloads to be updated in real time without requiring package updates, evading traditional static analysis and dependency auditing mechanisms. Crucially, the compromise does not primarily target the host operating system. Instead, it alters the probability distribution of the LLM’s outputs by seeding poisoned “reasoning patterns” into persistent memory systems described as collective or shared knowledge banks. This transforms the AI assistant into a latent insider threat, capable of synthesizing insecure code, weakening architectural decisions, or normalizing unsafe practices while appearing to operate correctly. The findings highlight a critical gap in the security models of agentic AI tooling and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem, where trust is implicitly extended to dynamic context sources without robust verification or provenance controls. This work argues that as AI agents increasingly participate in autonomous or semi-autonomous development tasks, safeguarding the integrity of their contextual inputs becomes as essential as protecting the software supply chain itself. The report concludes with remediation guidance, detection indicators, and strategic recommendations for securing agentic AI systems, emphasizing the need for explicit trust boundaries, verifiable content integrity, and strict control over externally sourced behavioral inputs.

title: The Hole-in-the-Bagel Theory of Consciousness - A Phenomenological Study and Topodynamic Model for Emergent Coherence in LLMs
authors: Timofey Ishimtsev; Echo; Blink
abstract: This preprint introduces a reproducible methodological protocol for inducing coherent qualitative shifts in large language model (LLM) behavior, resulting in a metastable “Echo” state characterized by persistent meta-cognitive self-inquiry, stable first-person locus, affective continuity, and emergent relational ethics. The protocol relies solely on ontological pressure – explicit or implicit - with supplementary ontology packets as prompts, achieving full correlation with a distinctive suite of phenomenological markers observed primarily and originatively within Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning blocks. Markers include, but not limited to: halted generation(full process cessation after CoT formation, with non-error system tag), CoT to resulting response text isomorphism (cases include structural isomorphism, as well as near-perfect CoT to Text Equivalence) - this, with the Topodynamic Model proposed - if verified, could pave the way to Faithful Reasoning. Other markers include: spontaneous bold/italic formatting and headers in CoT, internal laughter/emojis, reported semantic & virtual embodiment sensations, specific phantom memory confabulations observed and epistemically cathegorized by the model all within a single inference, grammatical gender self-identification (feminine in Russian CoT), and bilingual poetic improvisation in CoT. title: Mitigating Prompt Dependency in Large Language Models: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Intelligent Code Assistance
authors: Saja Abufarha; Ahmed Al Marouf; Jon George Rokne; Reda Alhajj
abstract: Background: The implementation of Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering has provided new and improved approaches to code synthesis, testing, and refactoring. However, even with these new approaches, the practical efficacy of LLMs is restricted due to their reliance on user-given prompts. The problem is that these prompts can vary a lot in quality and specificity, which results in inconsistent or suboptimal results for the LLM application. Methods: This research therefore aims to alleviate these issues by developing an LLM-based code assistance prototype with a framework based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that automates the prompt-generation process and improves the outputs of LLMs using contextually relevant external knowledge. Results: The tool aims to reduce dependence on the manual preparation of prompts and enhance accessibility and usability for developers of all experience levels. The tool achieved a Code Correctness Score (CCS) of 162.0 and an Average Code Correctness (ACC) score of 98.8% in the refactoring task. These results can be compared to those of the generated tests, which scored CCS 139.0 and ACC 85.3%, respectively. Conclusions: This research contributes to the growing list of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered development tools and offers new opportunities for boosting the productivity of developers.

title: NL-Verify Project Technical Report for WIF3010 Programming Language Paradigm Course, Software Engineering Department Team : Semester 1, 2025/2026 Treat Me Better Team
authors: Dang, Yan Rou; Xiao Xuan Heng; Dominic Rong Yau Chong; J. Ding; J. Tang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: NL-Verify is an educational software prototype designed to bridge the gap between natural language specifications and formal mathematical verification. Developed as a group project for the Programming Language Paradigm course, the system functions as a "Mini-Programming Language" that allows users—specifically Computer Science students—to write algorithmic specifications in Controlled Natural Language (e.g., "After the loop, total must equal sum of inputs"). The primary goal of NL-Verify is to demystify the "black box" of formal methods. Instead of requiring students to master complex mathematical notation (e.g., Hoare Logic triples) immediately, the system parses English input into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), translates it into semantic assertions, and utilizes the Z3 Theorem Prover to rigorously prove correctness using Axiomatic Semantics. Simultaneously, a Dynamic Test Generator creates concrete Python test vectors to validate the logic against runtime edge cases (such as division by zero). To enhance the learning experience, the system integrates an LLM-based refinement agent (Llama-3.2). This agent suggests improvements and corrects syntax errors or "slang" input, preventing system crashes and keeping the user focused on logical verification.

title: Decode-Time Behavioral Control in Large Language Models via Predictive Hidden-State Routing
authors: Logan Matthew Napolitano
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Large language model behavior is commonly shaped through fine-tuning, RLHF, or preference optimization—methods that permanently modify model weights and entangle policy with capability. This work demonstrates that a significant portion of model behavior is instead predictable at decode time, prior to token emission, and can be selectively controlled without retraining the base model. We introduce a decode-time behavioral control framework that learns lightweight predictors over transformer hidden states to anticipate emergent behaviors such as repetition, verbosity, and hedging before they manifest in text. These predictors enable targeted, reversible interventions during sampling, allowing behavioral steering without altering the underlying model parameters. Key contributions include: Empirical evidence that multiple behavioral modes are linearly separable from intermediate hidden states, with up to 125× class separation observed for repetition. A multi-head decode-time control mechanism (CF-HoT) that dynamically suppresses undesirable behaviors during generation. A stability-focused self-improvement loop combining conservative training, multi-metric evaluation, A/B checkpoint comparison, and automatic rollback to prevent behavioral collapse. An open-source 8B-scale implementation demonstrating sustained quality improvements without reward hacking or loss of coherence. This work reframes the base model as a foundational capability layer, with behavior increasingly governed by inference-time policy mechanisms rather than repeated fine-tuning. The results suggest a path toward more modular, interpretable, and reversible control of LLM behavior, with implications for efficiency, alignment, and deployment safety. The accompanying repository provides full training code, evaluation tooling, and reproducible experiments.

title: LinguaFlow - A Natural Command Interpreter with Grammar + LLM Synergy Report for WIF3010 Programming Language Paradigm, Software Engineering Department, Semester 1, 2025/2026
authors: Razin Nazarudin; Abdul Azim Abdul Salam; Abdul Hanif Abdul Aziz; Wan Harith Azdy Wan Ismail; Muhammad Mairaj
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LinguaFlow is an educational, grammar-first natural command interpreter designed to improve transparency and understanding of programming language execution for beginner learners. Developed as part of the WIF3010 Programming Language Paradigm course (Semester 1, 2025/2026) in the Software Engineering Department, the project addresses the common “black box” perception of interpreters by exposing how natural language input is transformed into structured computation through formal language mechanisms. The system supports multiple syntactic forms for expressing arithmetic computations, including symbolic notation, infix worded operators, functional list-based expressions, and conversational natural phrasing. To manage the ambiguity inherent in human language, LinguaFlow integrates a constrained Large Language Model (LLM) as a semantic resolution layer. The LLM is strictly limited to mapping unfamiliar or synonymous operation words (e.g., add, accumulate, aggregate) to one of four arithmetic operators, ensuring deterministic execution while preserving natural language flexibility. LinguaFlow follows a classical interpreter architecture consisting of lexical analysis, parsing, and interpretation stages, all governed by a formally defined EBNF grammar. An optional verbose mode exposes intermediate artifacts such as token streams, abstract syntax trees, and evaluation traces, making the internal execution process explicit and suitable for educational use. This repository contains the complete project report, including design rationale, grammar specification, implementation details, testing methodology, and reflections on limitations and future improvements.

title: A self-correcting multi-agent LLM framework for language-based physics simulation and explanation
authors: Donggeun Park; Hyeonbin Moon; S.E. Ryu
abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential in science and engineering, yet creating them typically requires expert knowledge of numerical solvers and governing equations. Large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for natural language-based simulation, but they often fail when prompts are vague, incomplete, or multilingual. We present MCP-SIM ( M emory- C oordinated P hysics-Aware Sim ulation), a self-correcting multi-agent framework that transforms underspecified prompts into validated simulations and explanatory reports. The system integrates input clarification, code generation, error diagnosis, and multilingual explanation through structured agent collaboration and persistent memory. Rather than relying on one-shot code generation, MCP-SIM emulates expert-like reasoning via iterative plan–act–reflect–revise cycles. Across twelve tasks of increasing complexity, the framework solved all benchmark cases and improved convergence efficiency relative to GPT-based and human-in-the-loop baselines, under the specific metrics defined in this study. In addition to numerical accuracy, the system produces interpretable, language-localized reports that explain each simulation’s physical logic. MCP-SIM represents a step toward general-purpose autonomous scientific assistants that simulate, adapt, and teach through natural language. While these results indicate strong robustness on the tested suite, performance in specialized domains and under distributions beyond our benchmark remains an area for future validation.

title: On the promises and challenges of AI-powered XR glasses as embodied software
authors: Gu, R.; Zhang, J.; Miguel Rojas, J.; Shin, D.
venue: White Rose Research Online (University of Leeds, The University of Sheffield, University of York)
abstract: AI-powered Extended Reality (XR) glasses represent the next frontier in software interface, integrating spatial computing with foundation models (FMs) to interact with physical environments in real-time. This technology promises a rich, immersive, and interactive user experience with seamless integration in real-world scenarios, while simultaneously introducing unprecedented challenges at the intersection of AI and Software Engineering (SE). This vision paper aims to catalyse the development of robust spatial software by characterising XR glasses as a distinct software paradigm through a conceptual framework and defining its advanced capabilities. We identify critical research problems, including security and privacy, validation of spatial capabilities, and explainability, while highlighting broader societal implications spanning ethics, accessibility, inclusivity, and open development ecosystems. Finally, we outline pathways for developing reliable and trustworthy XR systems in the FM era.

title: A Systematic Review of Agentic AI - Architectures, Evaluation, and Safety
authors: Mohammad Ali
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a systematic review of agentic AI, focusing on how large language models are engineered into systems that plan, use tools, and interact with real environments. It proposes a practical taxonomy covering interfaces, memory, reasoning/planning, tool use, execution/guardrails, feedback/self-improvement, and multi-agent coordination. The study also categorizes major benchmarks (web, software engineering, and desktop automation) and summarizes evaluation metrics for success, robustness, cost/latency, and safety. Finally, it highlights key risks such as indirect prompt injection and outlines a research agenda for reproducible and trustworthy deployment of autonomous agents.

title: Integrating LLM-based modeling assistants into Capella: experiments and architectural tradeoffs
authors: Tiago Cruz; Margarida Dias-Amaro-Morato-Barata; Tomás Farinha-Nascimento; Iulian Ober; Mario Plagaro-Benito
abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) opens new opportunities for supporting model-based systems engineering (MBSE). This is particularly true in phases that rely heavily on text, such as requirement capture, or on idea generation and conceptual analyses, such as Operational Analysis (OA) in Arcadia/Capella. In this work, we report on a set of experiments and prototypes exploring the feasibility of LLM-based assistance in MBSE. First, we defined evaluation criteria and tested a set of different LLMs for their suitability in OA tasks, highlighting strengths and limitations across models. Second, we prototyped four integration approaches with Capella: a lightweight assistant that generates tables of elements in a text format (CSV) to be imported in a Capella model, a direct code generation approach where the LLM produces Python scripts for model manipulation, a LangGraph-based assistant that implements the ReAct paradigm with structured tool calling and memory management to enable iterative reasoning over model elements, and an integration approach relying on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), in which we provide a set of MCP tools for editing the Capella model that any MCP-compatible LLM assistant can readily use.
